Ils s'accordent pour voir dans « صنع الله » une expression d'insistance, et dans « Il a rendu parfait toute chose » l'idée qu'Il a tout créé avec solidité et perfection, et qu'Il est informé de ce que vous faites. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi et d'autres rapportent la lecture de Hamza et de Hafs sur la forme verbale du verset suivant. Al-Qurtubi et al-Qushayri estiment que ce mouvement aura lieu au Jour dernier, tandis que al-Sha'rawi considère que la mobilité des montagnes suit celle de la terre et qu'elle n'est pas perceptible à l'œil humain. Ibn 'Ashur, lui, lit le verset comme une invitation à méditer sur l'ordre subtil de la création, sans y voir la ruine de l'univers. Ces lectures divergent surtout sur le moment où se produit ce mouvement, non sur sa perfection.

Ce passage de la sourate An-Naml décrit le sort des hommes le jour de la résurrection, lorsque le Cor sera soufflé : tous ceux qui sont dans les cieux et sur la terre seront saisis d'effroi, à l'exception de ceux que Dieu voudra épargner, et tous viendront à Lui humbles et soumis. On verra les montagnes, que l'on croit immobiles, passer comme passent les nuées, « œuvre de Dieu qui a tout parfaitement disposé ». Vient ensuite la rétribution : celui qui apporte une bonne action recevra mieux qu'elle, et il sera à l'abri de ce jour d'effroi ; celui qui apporte une mauvaise action aura le visage jeté dans le Feu. Les commentateurs, tels qu'Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, Mujahid et Qatada, s'accordent largement pour voir dans la bonne action la profession de foi « Il n'y a de divinité que Dieu », et dans la mauvaise action l'associationnisme, même si Qatada parle de la sincérité et Zayd ibn Aslam de l'accomplissement des obligations. Quant au « mieux qu'elle », Ibn Abbas l'explique par le bien qui parvient à l'auteur grâce à elle ; Ibn Jurayj et Ikrima estiment qu'aucune chose n'est meilleure que la profession de foi ; al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd et Muhammad ibn Ka'b y voient la multiplication par dix, et al-Razi l'interprète comme la contemplation du visage de Dieu. Les lectures diffèrent sur « effroi de ce jour », tantôt annexé, tantôt tanwin ; al-Farra' et Abu 'Ubayd préfèrent l'annexion, plus générale, tandis qu'Abu 'Ali al-Farisi estime que les deux lectures ont le même sens. Les exceptés de l'effroi sont, selon les avis, les martyrs (Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr), les anges (Muqatil) ou les houris (al-Dahhak). Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi tiennent pour deux soufflements, celui de l'effroi et de la mort, puis celui de la résurrection, tandis que d'autres en comptent trois. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi distinguent l'effroi de la stupeur devant les événements, que nul n'évite, de la crainte du châtiment, propre à ceux qui ont mal agi.

Ce verset décrit le sort de celui qui se présente au Jour de la Résurrection avec une mauvaise action, que la majorité des commentateurs identifient au polythéisme (chirk), comme le rapportent al-Tabari d'après Ibn Abbas, Mujahid et Qatada. Il fait pendant au verset précédent, où celui qui apporte la bonne action, pour eux la profession de foi « il n'y a de dieu que Dieu », reçoit mieux que ce qu'il a fait. Ceux qui rencontrent Dieu dans le polythéisme seront jetés au feu le visage contre terre, comme l'expliquent al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi et al-Nasafi, et on leur dira sur le ton du reproche : « Ne serez-vous rétribués que pour ce que vous faisiez ? »
La plupart des exégètes s'accordent à voir dans la mauvaise action le shirk, al-Shawkani et Ibn Ashur s'appuyant sur l'adresse faite aux coupables. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi expliquent que le visage est mentionné pour sa noblesse et que l'expression englobe tout le corps. Ibn Kathir précise que celui qui rencontre Dieu sans bonne action, ou dont les mauvaises actions l'emportent, subit le même sort. Al-Razi et al-Alusi rapportent que les Murji'a et les Mu'tazila ont tiré du verset des arguments sur le pécheur croyant, et al-Alusi répond que le terme désigne le shirk selon les salaf.
Ibn Ashur voit dans le verset une conclusion récapitulative des avertissements précédents, et Ibn Uthaymin estime que rétribuer par l'acte même est une forme d'équité, et retient que le mécréant est puni à la fois pour sa mécréance et pour ses péchés.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète de déclarer à son peuple qu'il a reçu l'ordre d'adorer le Seigneur de cette cité, c'est-à-dire La Mecque, Celui qui l'a rendue sacrée et sûre, où l'on ne doit verser aucun sang, ni opprimer personne, ni chasser son gibier, ni couper ses arbres. À Lui appartient toute chose, et il lui a été commandé d'être parmi les soumis à Dieu. Les commentateurs s'accordent à identifier la cité à La Mecque, et à voir dans l'attribution de cette cité au Seigneur un honneur qui la distingue. Ibn 'Abbas l'entend de La Mecque, tandis qu'Abu al-'Aliya y voit Mina, selon al-Mawardi. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir expliquent que le sacré désigne le respect de sa sainteté et l'interdiction d'y chasser ou d'y couper les arbres, et que la formule « et à Lui appartient toute chose » écarte l'idée que la seigneurie de Dieu se limiterait à cette cité.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baydawi rapportent que cette sacralisation est un bienfait divin pour les Quraychites, qui vivaient en sécurité dans une région troublée. Ibn 'Atiyya explique que l'attribution du sacré à Dieu renvoie à son décret et à Sa science préalable, tandis que la parole du Prophète attribuant ce sacré à Abraham renvoie à l'invocation et à la proclamation de ce dernier. Ibn Kathir précise que ce sacré est établi à la fois par le décret divin et par la loi religieuse.

Sur la suite du verset, les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le Prophète doit réciter le Coran, et que celui qui se guide le fait pour son propre bien, tandis que celui qui s'égare ne fait que causer son propre tort. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Nasafi rapportent que ce passage a été abrogé par le verset du combat, alors qu'Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Uthaymin estiment qu'il reste valable et qu'il ne s'agit pas d'un abrogation. Enfin, la promesse de montrer des signes est interprétée par Mujahid comme des signes dans le ciel, par al-Hasan comme ceux de l'au-delà, et par Ibn 'Atiyya comme des châtiments ici-bas comme celui de Badr.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète de déclarer qu'il a reçu l'ordre d'adorer le Seigneur de cette cité, qui l'a rendue sacrée et à qui appartient toute chose, d'être du nombre des soumis à Dieu, et de réciter le Coran. Celui qui se met sur la bonne voie n'en tire profit que pour lui-même, et celui qui s'égare n'a à subir que l'avertissement du Prophète. Les commentateurs s'accordent à identifier la cité comme La Mecque, et à expliquer que sa sanctuarisation signifie l'interdiction d'y combattre, de chasser son gibier et d'y couper ses arbres ; la mention de la seigneurie divine sur elle est un honneur, et la phrase « à Lui appartient toute chose » écarte l'idée que Sa souveraineté se limiterait à ce lieu. Ibn 'Abbas et al-Hasan rattachent cette sacralisation à la décision divine dès la création des cieux et de la terre ; al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya y voient une attribution à Dieu, car elle relève de Son décret et de Sa science, alors que le Prophète l'a attribuée à Abraham dans un hadith ; Ibn Juzayy et d'autres concilient les deux en disant qu'Abraham l'a fait connaître. Sur la récitation, al-Hasan y voit un appel à mettre le Coran en pratique, tandis qu'al-Shawkani et d'autres y voient une lecture accompagnée de suivi. Quant à la phrase « je ne suis qu'un avertisseur », al-Nahhas, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Suyuti la tiennent pour abrogée par le verset du combat, alors qu'Ibn Kathir et d'autres y voient l'accomplissement de la transmission du message. Les « signes » promis sont interprétés par Ibn 'Abbas et Mujahid comme des signes d'ici-bas, tels que la fumée et la fente de la lune ou la subsistance, par al-Hasan comme ceux de l'au-delà, et par al-Baghawi et d'autres comme la bataille de Badr. Plusieurs concluent que Dieu n'est jamais inattentif à ce que font les hommes.

Dieu ordonne à Son Messager de dire qu'il a reçu l'ordre d'adorer le Seigneur de cette cité, La Mecque, qui l'a rendue sacrée, à Lui appartenant toute chose, et d'être parmi les soumis à Dieu, puis de réciter le Coran. Celui qui se guide le fait pour lui-même, et celui qui s'égare, le Prophète n'a que la mission d'avertir. Il lui est ordonné de louer Dieu et de dire que Dieu leur montrera Ses signes, qu'ils reconnaîtront. Les commentateurs s'accordent à identifier la cité à La Mecque et son sanctuaire à la protection de ses lieux contre le combat, la chasse et la coupe des arbres, tout en divergeant sur l'étendue du sacré entre La Mecque et Mina, selon al-Mawardi. Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir expliquent que l'attribution de cette sacralisation à Dieu ne contredit pas la parole du Prophète attribuant la sacralisation à Abraham, celui-ci l'ayant proclamée par son invocation. Les versets suivants évoquent le rassemblement du jour dernier, le souffle dans le Cor et le sort des montagnes, ainsi que la récompense de la bonne action, que la plupart des exégètes identifient comme la profession de foi « Il n'y a de divinité que Dieu », et le châtiment du mal, qui est l'association à Dieu. Quant aux signes annoncés, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid et Muqatil y voient les événements d'ici-bas comme Badr, la fumée et la fente de la lune, al-Hasan les place dans l'au-delà, et Mujahid y voit aussi les signes dans les âmes et l'univers. Les lecteurs divergent sur la lecture de « ta'malun » à la deuxième personne ou à la troisième. Al-Nahhas et Ibn 'Ashur notent que certains tiennent le verset du glaive pour abrogeant la mission d'avertissement, opinion que ni Ibn Kathir ni Ibn 'Ashur n'adoptent. Tous s'accordent sur le fait que Dieu n'est jamais inattentif à ce que font les hommes.
en: The surah opens with the disjoined letters ṭ-s, whose precise meaning the commentators leave to God. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes them as an oath and a divine name, Qatada as a name of the Quran, and others as an abbreviation of al-Latif and al-Sami'. The verses state that these signs are those of the Quran, a clear Book that shows the attentive reader that it comes from God, and that no human or jinn can produce its like. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the 'clear Book' may refer to the Preserved Tablet, to the surah or to the Quran itself, and that its conjunction with the Quran works as the linking of two qualities; most commentators do not choose among these readings. There is broad agreement that 'guidance and glad tidings' describe the Quran and are reserved for believers: al-Tabari explains it as guidance away from error and good news of success in the afterlife, Yahya ibn Salam and al-Sha'bi as guidance to Paradise and reward, while others understand a general guidance offered to all. The passage then describes believers who establish prayer, give zakat and hold firm certainty about the Hereafter. Scholars differ on the repeated pronoun 'they': most see emphasis and restriction, while al-Zamakhshari treats the clause as a parenthesis. The text then turns to those who do not believe in the Hereafter, for whom their evil deeds are made to appear fair, who wander in confusion, who suffer a terrible punishment, and who are the greatest losers.

This verse states that the Qur'an is a guidance that shows the straight path and a glad tidings of reward for those who believe in it and accept what it contains. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the guidance as protection from error and the glad tidings as Paradise and success in the Hereafter. Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan explain that both words may be read as states, predicates or subjects, describing the verses as clear signs. The commentators agree that the believers meant are those who establish the prayer, pay the zakat and are certain of the Hereafter, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di link complete faith to these practices. On the meaning of guidance, Yahya ibn Sallam takes it as leading to Paradise, al-Sha'bi as deliverance from error, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that it increases the guidance of believers and that the glad tidings belong to them alone. Al-Sha'rawi argues that this is a divine help granted to believers, not merely an indication. Regarding alms, Ibn 'Ashur explains that it means charity in general, since the fixed zakat was prescribed only after the Hijra. As for the repetition of the pronoun in the phrase about certainty of the Hereafter, al-Zamakhshari reads it as stressing exclusivity, whereas others see it simply as emphasis. The overall meaning is that the Qur'an illuminates and gladdens those who believe in it and act upon it.

This passage presents the verses of this surah as guidance and good news for believers, and describes those believers as people who establish the prayer, give zakat, and are firmly certain of the Hereafter. The commentators explain that establishing the prayer means performing it with its obligations and recommended acts and keeping to its times. Most take zakat to mean the obligatory alms, though some say it means purifying the soul from the stains of sins. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the guidance as direction to the truth and the good news as success and reward in Paradise. Al-Sha'bi and Yahya ibn Sallam take guidance as protection from error and the good news as Paradise or reward.

Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the repeated pronoun in the phrase about certainty adds emphasis and limitation, so that only those who combine faith with good deeds reach true certainty, since fear of the consequence drives them to bear hardship. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi adopt this reading, while al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy treat the clause as part of the relative clause.

As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their deeds have been made attractive to them so that they see them as good, and so they wander in confusion, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, or recklessly persist, according to Abu al-Aliya, or play, according to Qatada. Ibn Atiyya suggests that this adornment may mean that desires were created in them. Many take the evil punishment to be the killing and capture at Badr, reported from Ibn Abbas and others, while others see it as the punishment of the Hereafter, and Ibn Kathir includes both this world and the next. Abu Hayyan notes that the phrase 'the greatest losers' is a superlative, meaning the disbeliever's loss in the Hereafter is greatest.

This verse states that those who do not believe in the Hereafter have their deeds made attractive to them, so that they see them as good and wander in bewilderment. The commentators agree on the meaning of 'ya'mahun', which denotes hesitation and wandering like one who has lost the way. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as hesitation, Abu al-'Aliya, Abu Malik and al-Rabi' as persistence in error, Qatada as playing, and al-Hasan as perplexity. On the attribution of the embellishment to God, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi keep it literal, holding that God creates in them the inclination that makes their deeds seem good, whereas al-Zamakhshari holds that attribution to God is figurative and attribution to Satan is literal. Al-Hasan, as reported by some, takes the deeds to be the good works they neglected. Regarding 'a painful punishment', most identify it with the killing and capture at Badr in this world, while others understand a general punishment in this life and the next. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan connect the verse to the idea that faith in the Hereafter is what drives complete good conduct. The commentators link this passage to the description of the Qur'an as guidance and good news for believers, before turning to the Prophet's receiving of it from a wise and knowing Lord.

This verse describes those who do not believe in the Hereafter: their evil deeds have been made attractive to them, so they see them as good, and they wander bewildered in their misguidance. The commentators differ on what this embellishment means. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di understand it as God's embellishment, a punishment for denying the Hereafter, which makes them love their evil deeds and leaves them to go further astray. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him hold that attributing it to God is figurative: it may mean that God let Satan act, or that long life and comfort led them to follow their desires. A view reported from al-Hasan takes it as the good deeds they were obliged to do, which they overlooked. As for the "evil punishment", most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Razi, identify it with killing and capture at Badr. Al-Alusi also allows that it refers to both this world and the next. The phrase "the greatest losers" is explained as being the greatest losers in the Hereafter, having lost the reward and deserved punishment; al-Razi offers two readings, losing oneself and losing one's place in Paradise. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the judgment targets a group defined by its denial, not specific individuals. The verse thus warns against indifference to the Hereafter and describes its consequences.

This verse states that the Prophet ﷺ receives the Quran from One who is All-Wise in His governance and All-Knowing of His creation. The commentators explain that the verb "tulaqqa" means that he is given the Quran and taught it, and that the verse serves as a preface to the stories of the prophets that follow in the surah. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it answers the Quraysh, who claimed that Muhammad had composed the Quran himself, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees in "min ladun" a clear statement that its source is divine. Al-Hasan al-Basri reads the verb as meaning receiving, Qatada as taking, and Ibn Juzayy as being given. The two attributes are commented on differently: al-Razi and Abu Hayyan link wisdom to practical rulings and knowledge to the broader scope of learning, whereas Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take them as praise of the depth of the prophetic knowledge. Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the indefinite form magnifies both the Giver and the Giver's attributes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin add that divine wisdom appears both in the rulings and in the events. The commentators therefore agree on the divine origin of the Quran and the greatness of the One who transmits it, while differing on the precise sense of the verb and on how the two attributes should be understood.

This passage recounts Moses journeying with his family from Madyan toward Egypt. Lost on a dark, cold night, he saw a fire in the distance and told his household that he would bring them news of the road or a burning brand to warm themselves. The commentators agree that the 'news' means directions, the 'shihab' is a flaming brand, and the cold is the reason for the request. The readings differ between the annexed form 'shihabi qabasin' and the nunated 'shihabin qabasin'. Al-Tabari holds both readings to be valid and close in meaning, reporting the grammatical arguments of the Basran and Kufan scholars; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the annexed form, while the Kufans read the second word as a substitute or qualifier. Al-Zamakhshari explains the future marker 'sa' as conveying certainty or the distance involved, and notes that another verse uses 'perhaps' to express hope. As for what follows, most commentators hold that the fire was in fact a divine light; on who is 'within the fire' they differ: God Himself according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the light, Moses, or the angels, while some take it as the blessing of the sacred ground. Ibn Kathir sees in it a consolation for the Prophet, who learns what befell the earlier messengers.

The commentators explain that Moses, travelling from Madyan to Egypt on a cold night when he had lost his way, saw a fire from afar and told his family he would bring them news of the road or a brand to warm themselves. When he reached it, he was called: blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory to God, Lord of the worlds. Most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan, hold that the one in the fire is God's light, or God Himself speaking to Moses from it, and that those around it are the angels; the fire is so called because Moses took it to be fire. Al-Tabari also reports that the blessing falls on the fire itself, or on Moses and the angels together, while al-Zamakhshari says it extends to all in the holy land of Syria. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi note that the fire was a light without flame, and Ibn Jarir says the phrase means those close to the fire rather than inside it. Readers differ on 'shihabin qabas', some reading with tanwin and others with the construct; Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the construct, which the grammarians treat as an annexation of kind. As for 'subhan Allah', commentators read it either as God declaring Himself free of any unfitting attribute or as Moses expressing wonder at what he saw. The passage then tells how Moses threw his staff, which became a swift serpent, and he fled; God reassured him that messengers do not fear in His presence, except one who has wronged and then repented, an exception most take as disconnected, though some take it as connected with Moses' earlier killing before his mission. He was then told to put his hand into his garment so that it came out white without blemish, one of nine signs sent to Pharaoh and his people.

God tells Moses that He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. The commentators explain that this means the Capable and Dominant who cannot be overcome, who governs His creation with wisdom. Ibn 'Abbas and others report that this address follows Moses seeing the fire in the tree; God calls him and tells him that whoever is in the fire and around it is blessed, and that He is exalted above all that is unfitting. The exegetes differ on who is meant by 'whoever is in the fire': according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr it is God Himself or His light; others say it is Moses; al-Sudi says the angels; some hold that the blessing returns to the fire itself or to the blessed place. As for the pronoun 'innahu', most take it as the pronoun of the matter, while some regard it as a mere grammatical support. All agree the passage prepares the miracles God will show through Moses. Then God orders him to throw his staff, which becomes a serpent moving like a jinn; Moses flees in fear, and God reassures him that messengers do not fear in His presence. Some exclude from this one who wronged and then repented; al-Tabari and Ibn Jurayj report that this refers to Moses himself, because of killing the Egyptian before his prophethood, while others consider the exception discontinuous. The commentators also mention nine signs, with the hand and the staff, sent to Pharaoh and his people, who were a corrupt folk. When the clear signs came to them they said it was manifest sorcery, and they denied them out of injustice and arrogance though their souls were certain of them.

This verse recounts Moses being commanded to throw his staff, which becomes a serpent moving swiftly like a jann, so he fled without turning back, and God reassures him that messengers do not fear in His presence. The commentators agree on the plain sense: reassuring Moses and removing his terror, and on the swiftness and size of the serpent. They also agree that "did not return" means he did not come back, as Mujahid said, or did not look back, as Qatada said. The main difference concerns the exception "except one who has done wrong." Al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Qutayba and al-Nahhas read it as a connected exception referring to the prophets themselves, citing Moses' killing of the Egyptian or prophets' sins followed by repentance. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a disconnected exception referring to other people; Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan prefer this reading because it brings good news to those who repent. Al-Farra' and others said that "illa" means "wa", but Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Qayyim rejected this view. The phrase "changed evil for good" is explained as repentance followed by righteous deeds. Al-Tabari and al-Razi note that the fear that remains for prophets after forgiveness is reverential awe rather than fear of punishment.

This passage from Surah al-Naml describes Moses seeing a fire on his journey to Egypt. God called him, declared the place blessed and identified Himself as the Mighty, the Wise, then ordered him to throw his staff, which became a quivering snake like a jinn; Moses fled without looking back, and God reassured him that the messengers have nothing to fear in His presence. On the exception "except one who has done wrong and then replaced evil with good," the commentators largely agree that the repentant is forgiven, but differ on its scope. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as a disjunctive exception referring to other people, while al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil read it as a connected exception concerning the prophets themselves, pointing to Moses' killing of the Egyptian; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi adopt this reading as an allusion to that event. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi explain that the repentant still fears out of reverence. Al-Farra' and some grammarians held that "illa" means "wa", a view al-Nahhas and Abu Hayyan rejected. Regarding the fire, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan understood it as God's light, while others took it as a real fire or as light without fire. Readings of "shihab qabas" differ without changing the core meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi reconcile the comparison of the staff to a jinn (for its speed) and to a great serpent (for its size) found elsewhere in the Quran.

The commentators explain that God commanded Moses to put his hand into his garment, and it would come out white without any blemish. This was one of nine signs sent to Pharaoh and his people, and God gives the reason: they were a people of transgressors, who had left obedience to God. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, reports that Moses wore a sleeveless woolen tunic, so the hand had to go through the collar, while others say only the palm entered the opening. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir add that the hand shone like lightning.

The scholars largely agree on the list of the nine signs: the staff, the hand, the years of drought and loss of crops, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, although Ibn Zayd adds the obliteration of wealth and Zamakhshari counts the splitting of the sea. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya explain that the word "mubsira" means clear and luminous, the act of seeing being attributed to the signs figuratively. All agree that Pharaoh and his people rejected these signs and called them sorcery, though inwardly they were certain of their truth, out of injustice and arrogance. Ibn Kathir sees in the story a warning to those who reject the Prophet Muhammad.

This verse tells that when Our clear and visible signs came to Pharaoh and his people, they called them manifest sorcery. The commentators agree that these are the nine signs given to Moses, and that the word "mubsira" (giving sight, clear) is applied to the signs themselves because they make the truth visible to whoever considers them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the denial ("juhud") meant rejecting the signs as coming from God, while "istiqan" refers to a firm inner certainty in their hearts. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi note that attributing sight to the signs is a figurative usage, since it is the onlookers who actually see. Ali ibn al-Husayn and Qatada read "mabsara", meaning a place where much seeing occurs. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi link the pairing of injustice and arrogance to refusing faith out of pride, and Ibn Atiyya observes that theologians have debated whether one can knowingly deny a truth one recognises. Al-Razi stresses that mentioning the souls shows that they denied with their tongues while being convinced in their hearts. The verse closes by directing attention to the fate of the corrupters, a warning addressed to the Prophet and to his contemporaries.

This passage of Surah An-Naml describes how Pharaoh and his people reacted when Moses brought clear, illuminating signs. They called them plain sorcery and denied them outwardly, yet their souls were certain that the signs came from God. Al-Tabari explains the denial (juhud) as rejection, the wrongdoing (zulm) as aggression, and the haughtiness (uluw) as pride. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the verb istayqana, meaning to be fully certain, is stronger than the simple form, and that the clause that follows is a circumstantial clause. These commentators agree that their rejection came from stubbornness rather than doubt. Ibn Atiyya discusses at length whether someone can know the truth and reject it out of obstinacy; he does not settle the matter, while others such as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy stress the deliberate nature of their offence. On the phrase 'see how was the end of the corrupters', the commentators differ on the addressee: most take it as addressed to the Prophet, peace be upon him, while others read it as a general call to reflect. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say this end was drowning in the sea, and al-Baydawi adds that the punishment in the hereafter will be burning. Modern commentators such as Ibn Uthaymin and al-Sha'rawi take the verse as a warning against arrogance and as a lesson from history. The verse contains no legal ruling; it serves as a warning to anyone who rejects the truth despite knowing it.

This verse tells us that Dawud and Sulayman were given a particular knowledge, and that they thanked God for preferring them over many of His believing servants. The commentators explain that this knowledge included judgement, wisdom and understanding the speech of birds, and that the indefinite word "knowledge" is taken either as magnificent or as partial. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that the use of "and they said" rather than "then they said" shows that gratitude must be expressed through deeds as well as words, and that knowledge is among the greatest blessings. Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the "many" are those who did not receive knowledge equal to theirs, while others take it to mean those with no knowledge at all. Al-Razi understands the knowledge to be the knowledge of God and His attributes. On Sulayman's inheritance from Dawud, most commentators, such as al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim, take it to mean prophethood and kingship rather than wealth, since prophets do not pass on their property and since Dawud had many other sons. Al-Hasan al-Basri, however, understood it as material inheritance, and Ibn Atiyya saw a figurative transfer of rule. The commentators report that Sulayman understood the speech of birds and that the wind carried to him the words of the ant, and Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Uthaymin voiced caution about the details of these reports. All agree on the meaning of his prayer: he asked God to help him give thanks for His favours and to count him among the righteous.

This verse says that Solomon's armies, made up of jinn, humans and birds, were gathered for him on a march and kept in good order, so that the first ranks were held back until the last ones caught up. Al-Tabari prefers this meaning of restraining, drawing on the Arabic sense of wazi' as one who holds back, and he is followed by many commentators. Ibn Abbas and Qatada say that the first were turned back toward the last so that none would run ahead, as kings do. Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean the ordering of ranks, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil take it as driving forward, and al-Hasan as pushing back. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya draw from it the lesson that rulers need officials who restrain the people from wrongdoing. The reports about the size of the host, such as the hundred farsakhs of encampment or the crystal dwellings that Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari relate, are judged by Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di to be unreliable or unverifiable, so they prefer to keep to the general sense of vast and well-ordered power. Al-Razi and al-Alusi discuss the reason for the birds' inclusion without settling the question. Ibn Uthaymin highlights the organisation and the careful command of the host, which he sees as the core of the verse.

These verses describe the march of Solomon's army, made up of jinn, humans and birds, whose ranks were organised so that the last rejoined the first. Coming to a valley known for its ants, an ant called on her companions to enter their dwellings, fearing that Solomon and his troops would crush them without noticing. Solomon smiled and laughed at her words, then prayed that God would inspire him to give thanks for the blessings given to him and to his parents, to do righteous deeds that please Him, and to admit him by His mercy among the righteous. The commentators agree that Solomon inherited from his father prophethood and kingship, not wealth, and that knowing the speech of birds was a divine favour. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that the ant was not only warning of physical crushing but also excusing an army that meant no harm. The location of the valley is disputed: Qatada and Muqatil place it in Syria, while Ka'b places it near Taif, and no decisive proof settles the matter. Opinions also differ on the ant itself: Nawf says the ants were the size of wolves, while al-Sha'bi says she had two wings, with no consensus. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the prohibition on killing ants is established in the Sunna, and that many stories about the ant's name or size come from Israelite reports. Some exegetes take the verse to show that animals have a form of speech, while others keep to the text without elaborating.

This passage of Surat an-Naml tells how Solomon, peace be upon him, heard an ant warn her companions that he and his armies might crush them without noticing, and smiled, laughing at her wit and the soundness of her words. The commentators agree on the apparent meaning: Solomon thanks God for the knowledge of the speech of birds and for the subjection of jinn, men and birds under his command. He asks his Lord to inspire him to give thanks for His favours to him and to his parents, to help him do righteous deeds that please Him, and to admit him by His mercy among His righteous servants. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others read this as an acknowledgement of a special grace and a fear of pride.

They differ on where the valley lies: Qatada and Muqatil place it in Syria, while Ka'b places it near al-Ta'if. They also differ over the ant: al-Kalbi and Qatada describe her as large, the size of a wolf or a sheep, while others take her to be an ordinary ant, and no firm conclusion is reached. Al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi relate reports about the laughter of prophets and the name of the ant, but Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin consider such reports, drawn from Israelite traditions, unestablished and not worth dwelling on. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith forbidding the killing of the ant, and jurists discuss whether it may be killed when it causes harm.

Grammarians also debate the function of the word "dahikan" (laughing): some take it as a circumstantial complement that reinforces the meaning, others as a description of the state. The sense remains the same: Solomon's smile went beyond a mere smile into a measured laugh, fitting for a prophet.

The commentators relate that Solomon, travelling with his armies of jinn, humans and birds, inspected the birds and found the hoopoe missing. He wondered why he could not see it, and whether it was among the absent, and threatened to punish it severely, to slaughter it, or to have it bring a clear justification. On why the hoopoe was singled out, opinions differ: al-Tabari reports that it guided Solomon to water, according to Ibn Abbas and others, while al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi add that it shaded him from the sun, and Wahb ibn Munabbih says it had missed its customary turn. Al-Tabari concludes that God did not specify the reason and that he cannot decide among them. As for the punishment, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Juraij said it meant plucking its feathers, others mentioned exposure to the sun, confinement with its natural enemies, or being left for ants, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note that the severe punishment is left undefined. The commentators agree that sultan means evidence or valid excuse, and that Solomon did not pass sentence before hearing it. When the hoopoe returned, it said it had learned what Solomon did not know, and brought news of a queen of Sheba who worshipped the sun with her people. Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud read this as the hoopoe defending its absence and justifying itself.

The commentators relate that Solomon, peace be upon him, inspected the birds during his journey and found the hoopoe missing. He threatened it with a severe punishment, or slaughter, unless it brought him a clear excuse. They differ on the nature of that punishment: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be plucking its feathers and leaving it exposed to the sun or to ants; Muqatil ibn Hayyan says it would be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun; others mention confining it with a creature of opposite nature, or separating it from its mate. As for why Solomon sought it, Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Salam report that the hoopoe showed him water in the desert, while Wahb ibn Munabbih says it had failed its customary turn in the king's presence. Al-Tabari, without deciding, considers either reason possible. When the hoopoe returned, it said it had learned what Solomon did not know: it had come from Saba with certain news of a queen who ruled its people, had a great throne, and she and her people prostrated to the sun instead of God, the devil having made their deeds seem fair and barred them from the path. The commentators read the phrase 'that they should not prostrate' in different ways grammatically, with al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya offering different analyses. They agree the hoopoe is praised for its knowledge of monotheism, but differ on its source; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari attribute it to divine inspiration. Ibn Kathir and others caution against accepting in full the Israelite narratives about the details of this story, and advise sticking to what the Quran says.

The commentators report that Solomon reviewed the birds, did not find the hoopoe, and threatened to punish it severely or slaughter it unless it brought a clear excuse. Not long after, the hoopoe returned and said: 'I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba with certain news.' The commentators agree that this means it knew what Solomon did not, that Saba is a tribe or town in Yemen, and that its ruler, a woman, governs them, is given every kind of resource and has a great throne, while she and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God. The exegetes debated at length the name and lineage of this queen and the details of her throne, matters on which the text is silent. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that ihata means knowing a thing from all its sides, and that the words alert Solomon that the weakest creature may know what others do not, so that the learned will not become conceited. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that the hoopoe saw what Solomon and his soldiers had not seen. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a special knowledge given by inspiration, and reads the encompassing as a figure for comprehensive knowledge. As for the phrase 'that they should not prostrate to God', the majority reading uses the doubled lam, while al-Kisa'i reads it as an imperative. The commentators differ on where the sentence stops and how it connects to what precedes it. On whether the bird perceives water beneath the earth, opinions differ: some say it sees the water and points it out, others consider this unfounded, since Solomon had jinn able to dig.

The hoopoe tells Solomon that he has found a woman ruling the people of Sheba, who has been given of everything a king needs, and who has a mighty throne. The commentators agree that this woman is the Queen of Sheba, Bilqis, and that her people worshipped the sun instead of God, so Satan adorned their deeds and turned them from the right path. The hoopoe thus shows that prostration belongs to God alone, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth and knows what is concealed and what is displayed. On the meaning of the words, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the throne as a royal seat, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention that it may mean kingship or an assembly. For the word khab', several say it refers to rain and plants, others to the hidden in general; al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi treat these words as the hoopoe's own speech. On the reading of alla without doubling, reported from al-Kisa'i and others, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that it makes prostration obligatory at that point. Many details transmitted, such as the name of the queen's father, the description of her throne or the stories about her mother, are not established, and several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di, prefer to keep to the Qur'anic text. All agree that associating others with God is wrongdoing.

The hoopoe tells Solomon, peace be upon him, that he found a woman ruling the people of Sheba in Yemen, who has been given everything a king needs and has a mighty throne. He saw that she and her people prostrate to the sun instead of to God, and that Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and barred them from the path, so they are not guided. The commentators agree that the prostration meant is worship of the sun, that Satan is the cause of this deviation, and that the hoopoe condemns it because they neglected to bow to God alone. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the woman as Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil, while others give different names. On the throne, Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil describe it as gold set with jewels, Qatada speaks of pearl legs, and al-Zamakhshari holds that its greatness is relative to the thrones of the kings of its time, while the Throne of God is incomparably greater than all creation. Readers differ over the word alla yasjudu: most read it with a shadda, al-Kisa'i reads it without, and al-Zajjaj concludes that this reading makes the recitation prostration obligatory, a view adopted by al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi. Accounts of the hoopoe's ability to see water underground are reported by the commentators without a unanimous verdict on their authenticity.

This passage recounts the story of the hoopoe and Solomon, peace be upon him. When Solomon inspected the birds and did not find the hoopoe, he threatened to punish it severely or slaughter it unless it brought a clear excuse. The hoopoe stayed a short while, then returned and told Solomon that it had grasped what he had not, and brought from Sheba a certain report: a woman rules over them, she has been given everything, and she has a mighty throne, and she and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God, Satan having made their deeds seem fair and turned them from the path. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, agree on the apparent meaning: a rebuke for prostrating to other than God, and the affirmation that God alone brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and earth and knows what is secret and what is shown. They differ on the meaning of khab': Mujahid and Ibn Zayd took it to mean rain and plants, Qatada to mean the secret, and others to mean anything hidden. They also differ on the reading of alla. Most read it with shadda, meaning so that they would not prostrate, linking it to what precedes; al-Kisai and Abu Ja'far read it with takhfif, meaning O people, prostrate, as a new command. Al-Zajjaj held that the recitation prostration is obligatory on the second reading, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi held that it is obligatory on both. Some take the verse as the hoopoe's speech, others as God's words. The passage closes with: God, there is no god but Him, Lord of the mighty Throne, and Ibn Kathir notes that the Throne is the greatest of creations.

This passage in the story of the hoopoe and Solomon (peace be upon him) reports what the hoopoe saw in Saba: a woman rules over them, she has been given of everything, she has a mighty throne, and she and her people prostrate to the sun instead of Allah. The commentators explain that Satan made their deeds seem attractive to them and turned them from the right path. Then comes the verse, 'that they should not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth.' The readings differ: the doubled form 'an la yasjudu' and the lightened form, which is a command to prostrate. Al-Tabari judges both readings to be well attested and both meanings correct. Most exegetes take al-khab' to mean rain in the sky and plants on the earth, while others take it as anything hidden. The general sense is the acknowledgement that Allah alone deserves worship, since He brings out what is hidden and knows both the secret and the open. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the hoopoe must not be killed, and note that many details transmitted from Israelite sources about the queen's throne and affairs have no basis in the Quran. As for 'Lord of the mighty throne,' it answers the greatness of the queen's throne, since Allah's throne is the greatest of creatures. Several scholars count this verse among the prostration verses, since one reading is a command and the other a rebuke to those who omit it.

Solomon tells the hoopoe that he will examine what it has reported, to see whether it is truthful or one of the liars. The apparent meaning is that he will test the report before believing it. The commentators explain that Solomon sends the hoopoe with a letter to the Queen of Sheba, ordering it to drop the letter to them and then withdraw nearby to listen to what they say to one another. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari relate that the bird delivered the letter through an opening in the palace, that the queen read it and then gathered her chiefs to consult them, as al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi also report. Most exegetes hold that the phrase "were you among the liars" is stronger than "did you lie", since it implies that lying is a habit of the speaker. Ibn Ashur adds that the wording also serves to frighten the hoopoe and deter it from repeating such conduct. Al-Zamakhshari understands the verb "nazara" as reflection rather than sight. On the word order, al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd speak of an inversion, so that the sense is: deliver it, then watch what they answer, then withdraw, while others keep the apparent sequence. The commentators do not settle these questions, and each reading has its grammatical and contextual support.

According to the commentators, after the hoopoe reported to Solomon about Bilqis and her people who bow down to the sun instead of God, Solomon wished to test whether his report was true. He wrote a letter and told the bird to drop it before them and then withdraw nearby to see what they would say to one another. There is broad agreement on the apparent meaning: a withdrawal close enough to hear. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the hoopoe dropped the letter before Bilqis; Ibn Kathir adds that the letter began with the basmala and that the words 'it is from Solomon' identified its sender. For 'do not exalt yourselves against me', al-Tabari, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it to mean do not be arrogant, Qatada to mean do not oppose, and Yahya ibn Salam to mean do not refuse. On word order, al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd allow an inversion: drop it, watch what they return, then withdraw. Most commentators keep the natural order, with withdrawal before observation, the observation being listening to their exchanges. Ibn Ashur sees the letter as a means of communication between realms, like a carrier pigeon. Al-Shawkani takes the watching to mean reflecting on what they say to one another. Several commentators note that opening a letter with the basmala is commendable, and that brevity that keeps its meaning clear is a mark of eloquence. On the place of withdrawal, some say the bird should hide, others that standing near without being seen suffices. No dissenting ruling is given on the letter itself.

This verse reports the words of the Queen of Sheba to her chiefs: a noble letter has been delivered to her. She then states its contents: it is from Solomon, it opens with the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, and it bids them not to exalt themselves against him and to come to him in submission. The commentators agree that al-Mala' refers to the notables and leading men of the people. On why the letter is called noble, opinions differ: al-Suddi says it was sealed, Qatada says its content was excellent, and Ibn Zayd says it came from a noble king; others add that it opened with the basmala or that it reached her in an unusual way. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the letter was brief, like the writings of the prophets, and that Solomon was the first to write the basmala, though Ibn Kathir judged the hadith on this point weak. On the grammar of 'innahu' and 'an la ta'lu', al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan propose several analyses, explanatory or appositional. Ibn Ashur notes that the letter was in a language the queen understood, and that the prohibition on exalting oneself carries the force of a threat. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn Ashur stress the concision and precision of Solomon's wording. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that 'Muslimin' means submitting, while noting that the exact sense, whether submitting to God or to Solomon, remains debated. The verse gives no further details of the delivery, which the commentators describe in various ways.

This passage gives Salomon's letter to the Queen of Sheba as Bilqis relayed it to her people. Most commentators explain that her words "It is from Solomon" mean the letter comes from him, and "and it begins with the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" mean its text opens with the basmala. They largely agree that "do not exalt yourselves over me" means not to be arrogant or to refuse his call, and "come to me in submission" means to come as obedient believers in the one God.

Opinions differ on why the letter is called "noble". Al-Sudi said because it was sealed, Qatada because of the goodness of its content, and Ibn Zayd because it came from a noble king. Al-Mawardi reports other reasons, such as that it was carried by the hoopoe. The meaning of "muslimin" also varies: al-Kalbi takes it as submitting, Ibn Abbas as monotheists, Sufyan as obedient, and Zuhayr as sincere.

Most note that the letter was very brief, like the letters of the prophets, and that Solomon was the first to open his letters with the basmala. Ibn Kathir considered the narration that the Prophet did the same after this verse to be weak in its chain. Grammarians also debate whether the "an" in "do not exalt yourselves" is explanatory, verbal, or an apposition to the letter.

The commentators explain these verses from Surah an-Naml, in which Solomon writes to the Queen of Sheba, telling her and her people not to exalt themselves against him but to come to him in submission. According to Ibn Abbas and most exegetes, "do not rise up against me" means "do not be arrogant"; Qatada takes it as "do not oppose me", Ibn Zayd as "do not behave as kings do", and Yahya ibn Salam as "do not refuse the summons". As for "come to me as Muslims", al-Kalbi understands it as "submitting", Ibn Abbas as "affirming God's oneness", Sufyan as "obedient", and others as "sincere".

The exegetes agree that the letter opened with the basmala, and that the messages of prophets were brief. They differ on why the letter is called "noble": al-Suddi says because it was sealed, Qatada because of the beauty of its contents, Ibn Zayd because of the nobility of its sender, and others mention that the hoopoe was made to carry it or other reasons.

Grammarians disagree on the role of "an" in "an la ta'lu". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read it as an explanatory particle, while Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat it as an apposition to "kitab" or as a complement. Al-Razi argues that the hoopoe's message was itself a miracle sufficient to establish God's oneness and prophethood, so no blind imitation was demanded.

Some commentators relate lengthy accounts of what followed, including the queen's gift. Much of this material derives from Israelite traditions, and Ibn Sa'di cautions that what the Quran does not establish should not be treated as part of the interpretation.

Balqis asks her chiefs for counsel about Solomon's letter and says she will decide nothing without their presence. They reply that they have numbers and strength, and leave the decision to her. The commentators explain that the word fatwa here means a judgment or counsel on a matter, that qati'a amran means to decide and settle, and that tashhadun means to be present. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that she wanted to learn their resolve and win their support. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi note that the chiefs first offered to fight and then placed the choice in her hands. Ibn Kathir adds that she then turned toward a peaceful settlement. On the phrase "and so they do", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj take it as God's own words confirming her statement, while al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as her own words stressing her point. Ibn Mas'ud's reading "qadiya" instead of "qati'a" is noted without being treated as a difference in meaning. The scholars draw from this passage mainly the principle of consultation in public affairs, and the right of an adviser to state his view respectfully before leaving the decision to the one who rules.

The Qur'an reports that the Queen of Sheba gathered the chiefs of her people to consult them about the letter she had received from Solomon. They replied that they possess strength, numbers and great valour in battle, and they left the decision to her, to command as she sees fit. Most commentators read this as a hint that they are ready to fight if she orders it, while placing the final judgement in her hands. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others cite figures for her forces attributed to Mujahid and Ibn Abbas, but Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir consider these numbers exaggerated or weakly transmitted, and several other authors do not rely on them.

The commentators differ on the meaning of strength. Ibn Zayd and Abu Hayyan take it to mean readiness for war, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi separate bodily and material strength from courage and steadfastness in combat, a distinction that al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also draw.

The queen, according to the commentators, did not choose war. She explains that when kings enter a town they ruin it and humiliate its nobles. The commentators differ on who speaks the phrase "and thus they do": Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi take it as God's confirmation of her words, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy take it as her own emphasis. She then chooses to send a gift, which Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir present as a test: if Solomon accepts it he is a king, and if he refuses it he is a prophet. Qatada, quoted by Ibn Kathir, praises her wisdom. The details of the gift remain disputed, and several authors do not treat them as established.

This verse records the words of the Queen of Sheba to her chiefs when she asks their counsel about Solomon's letter. They offer to fight, and she replies that when kings enter a town by force they ruin it and humiliate its noblest people through killing, captivity or enslavement, and that this is their constant custom. The commentators differ on the phrase "and so they do": al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Abbas take it as God's confirmation of her words, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Ashur take it as her own words, stressing an established habit of kings. They broadly agree that this warning prepares her decision to avoid confrontation through a peaceful gesture, sending a gift to test Solomon's intentions. Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi report that the chiefs first displayed their strength before leaving the decision to her. The details of the gift, its quantity and nature, and the tests Solomon set for the envoys are reported at length by al-Baghawi, al-Tha'labi and others from varied sources; Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di regard much of this as drawn from Israelite narratives that cannot be relied upon. It is nonetheless agreed that the gift was substantial and that Solomon refused it, declaring that what God has given him is better than what they possess.

The verse reports the words of the Queen of Sheba, who consults the leading men of her people about Solomon. She says she will send him a gift and wait to see what her messengers bring back: if he accepts it, he is a king seeking worldly goods; if he refuses, he is a prophet whom money cannot sway. The commentators agree on the general sense: the gift is offered to win favour and to test the recipient, and the envoys form a group led by a chief. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others report that the gift included male and female servants dressed alike so that boys could not be told from girls; others add gold bricks, jewels and mounts. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, however, consider many of these details to come from Israelite narratives, and none of them can be asserted with certainty. Opinions on the number differ: a hundred of each sex according to Ibn Abbas, two hundred according to Mujahid, five hundred according to Wahb. As for the test, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak see it as a sign: accepting the gift would show kingship, refusing it prophethood, while as-Suddi, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr explain it as distinguishing boys from girls by how they wash. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the queen was not sure of acceptance and wanted to clarify Solomon's intention. Al-Qurtubi recalls that the Prophet accepted gifts and explains Solomon's refusal by his wanting not goods but adherence to the religion. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn Uthaymin see the gift as a shrewd test based on indications, without vouching for the detailed narratives.

This passage describes the arrival of the envoys of the Queen of Sheba before Solomon, bearing her gift. Solomon rebukes them: will you provide me with wealth? What God has given me, prophethood and kingship, is better than what He has given you; it is you who rejoice in your gift, for you are people who boast of and vie over worldly things. The commentators agree that Solomon did not seek riches and that he was denouncing people's attachment to this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari report that Solomon refused the gift, sent the envoys back, and threatened them with armies they could not withstand and with expulsion from their land in humiliation and subjection unless they came to him as Muslims. The reports differ on the nature of the gift. Ibn Jarir, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd relate that it included boys and girls dressed alike, to test whether Solomon could tell them apart; al-Samani and Ibn Kathir relate that he distinguished them by the way they washed, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi regard these accounts as Israelite narratives whose truth cannot be affirmed. Ibn Kathir considers the most sound version to be that of gold vessels. Al-Zamakhshari mentions a far larger gift. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur see the refusal as a response to the queen's scheme to turn Solomon away from his call to Islam.

This passage records that Solomon, having rejected the gift of the Queen of Sheba, warns her envoys that he will come against them with armies they cannot withstand, and will drive them from their land humbled and abased if they do not come to him in submission. The commentators agree that these armies are Solomon's forces of jinn, men and birds, and that « la qibala lahum » means they have no power to resist them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that humiliation (adhilla) means losing the honour and rule they enjoyed, while saghar means enslavement and captivity; al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya repeat this distinction. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that the envoy conveyed the threat to the queen. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir, citing Qatada and others, say the queen then understood that Solomon was no ordinary king and that she could not withstand him, which led her to set out towards him. According to al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan, the pronoun in « minha » refers to the land of Saba. Ibn Kathir notes that much of the detail about these events comes from Israelite narratives. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as a threat meant to deter the queen from opposing Solomon. The commentators differ mainly on the exact scope of the threat, not on its general meaning.

The commentators explain that after Solomon sent back the gift of the Queen of Sheba, he asked his notables which of them would bring him her throne before she came to him in submission. A jinn ifrit offered to bring it before Solomon rose from his judgment seat, and one who had knowledge of the Book offered to bring it before Solomon's glance returned to him, and the throne was set before him in an instant. The commentators agree that the apparent meaning is a request to bring the throne before the queen arrived as a Muslim, with the aim of showing a sign of God's power and the truth of Solomon's prophethood, a view favoured by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. They differ on his motive: Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and others say he wished to show her a sign confirming his prophecy; Qatada says he feared that she would convert and her property would then become unlawful for him to take; Ibn Zayd says he wanted to test her intelligence by having the throne altered. They also differ on the identity of the one with knowledge of the Book: Ibn Abbas and most exegetes name Asaf ibn Barkhiya, Qatada names Malikha, Ibn Zayd a righteous man from an island in the sea, while others say it was Solomon himself. Most report that the Greatest Name of God was invoked and the throne moved in an instant, though they differ on how this happened. Some exegetes simply record these opinions without choosing among them, and others note that details beyond the text come from Israelite reports.

The verse tells how an ifrit, a strong and cunning jinn, offered to bring the throne of the Queen of Sheba to Solomon before he rose from his seat of judgment. He claimed he was strong enough to carry it and trustworthy enough to take nothing from it. The commentators agree that the ifrit is a powerful and crafty demon, but they differ on his name: Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Jubba'i give several names such as Kawzan or Dhakwan, while Ibn Abbas reports Sakhr, though none of these is firmly established. On the length of the session, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the judgment sitting from morning until midday, while Ibn Atiyya understands it as the moment of rising. On the word amin, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd explain that he would not diminish or alter the throne, and Ibn Abbas also mentions trustworthiness regarding a woman's private parts, a view others do not adopt. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see in the episode a display of God's power and a proof of Solomon's prophethood. The following part, in which the man with knowledge of the Book accomplishes the transfer, is attributed by most to Asaf ibn Barkhiya, a righteous servant who knew the Greatest Name of God, while others assign it to Solomon himself, to Gabriel, to al-Khidr, or to an ordinary man of the time. These differences concern identity and detail rather than the general sense of the speed of the transfer.

This verse recounts how a man who had knowledge of the Scripture promised Solomon that he would bring him the throne of the Queen of Sheba before his glance returned to him. When Solomon saw it set firmly before him, he said that this was a bounty from his Lord to test him, whether he would be thankful or ungrateful. He explained that whoever gives thanks does so for his own benefit, and whoever is ungrateful harms no one, for his Lord is self-sufficient and generous. The commentators agree that the throne was moved from Yemen to Syria in an instant, by a power granted to the one who held this knowledge. They differ, however, on his identity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, following Ibn Abbas and most scholars, name Asaf ibn Barakhya, a righteous man who knew the Greatest Name. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya mention Gabriel or another angel; Ibn Zayd and Ibn Lahi'a say it was al-Khidr; Qatada names him Malikha; Ibn al-Munkadir holds that it was Solomon himself, a view al-Razi considers the closest to the wording. There is also disagreement over the Book: some read it as the Preserved Tablet, others as the revealed scriptures, and Ibn Ashur as knowledge gained through wisdom. The phrase 'before your glance returns' is taken by Mujahid to mean the time one can gaze without blinking, while many see it as an image of speed. The invocation used is reported in several forms, such as 'O Living, O Self-Subsisting' or 'O Lord of Majesty and Honour'. Commentators note that gratitude binds and increases blessings and benefits the one who gives thanks, and Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn Uthaymin explain that Solomon's words refer specifically to ingratitude for this particular favour.

The commentators explain that when Solomon was brought the throne of Bilqis before her arrival, he ordered his men to alter it in order to test her perception: would she recognise it despite the change? They differ on how it was altered. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima speak of additions and removals, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid mention stripping its jewels or changing their colours, Qatada reports that its top was made its bottom, and Abu Salih mentions fish figures placed on it. As for the word "tahtadi", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean recognising the throne, while al-Razi and others read it as her ability to discern.

The commentators agree in praising the subtlety of Bilqis's answer, "as if it were it", which al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take as a sign of wisdom: she neither affirms nor denies. They differ on who speaks the phrase "we were given knowledge before her": most attribute it to Solomon and his people, while some attribute it to Bilqis. Regarding the "sarh", al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi describe a glass palace over water, which she mistook for a pool, which is why she lifted her garment. Ibn Kathir stresses that most of the accounts about her legs, the baths and the marriage come from Israelite traditions and should not be treated as reliable.

This verse recounts the test Solomon set for the Queen of Sheba: he ordered that her throne be altered in appearance to examine her judgment. When she arrived and was asked whether this was her throne, she answered that it was as if it were it, a careful reply that neither confirms nor denies. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi attribute the words that follow, 'We were given knowledge before her and we were submitters,' to Solomon and his companions, who thank God for having been guided first, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take them to be the queen's own words continuing her reply. Several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, explain that the phrase 'as if it were' expresses near-certainty without a categorical claim, which shows her prudence. On the meaning of the verb nakkirū, al-Baghawi, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir report differing views: removing the jewels, reversing top and bottom, changing the colours, or adding and subtracting parts. The commentators also note that the reason she had not believed before was her upbringing among a people who worshipped the sun. Many accounts about the glass palace, the queen's legs and her marriage to Solomon are described by Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin as Israelite narratives that should not be relied on in explaining the verse.

This part of the verse says that what she worshipped instead of God kept her from faith: it was the sun, and she had grown up among a disbelieving people. Most commentators agree on this reading. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take the worship of the sun to be what kept her from turning to Islam, with the phrase "she was of a disbelieving people" giving the reason, since she could not openly profess faith among her people until she came under Solomon's rule. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, whom al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer, hold that these words belong to Solomon's speech, recalling the knowledge given to him and his people before her. Some commentators allow that the subject of the verb could be God or Solomon, with the verb then taking a direct object without a preposition, an option Abu Hayyan and others find weak. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note the reading "annaha", which can make the clause an apposition or a cause. Ibn 'Ashur adds that disbelief had taken root in her through inheritance and upbringing. Al-Razi observes that the Mu'tazilite argument drawn from this verse does not hold under either reading.

This passage describes the moment the Queen of Sheba, Bilqis, enters the palace Solomon had prepared for her. She is told to enter the sarh; taking it for a deep expanse of water, she lifts her garments to wade through. Solomon tells her it is not water but a smooth palace of glass, and she responds: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds." The commentators agree that the purpose of the palace was to display the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and to confirm his prophethood, and that Bilqis embraced faith after witnessing these signs. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the sarh was a pool of water covered with glass, with fish swimming beneath, and that her lifting of the legs was to keep them dry. On the reason for building it, opinions differ: Wahb ibn Munabbih and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say Solomon wished to test her intelligence and see her legs, since the jinn claimed her legs were like a donkey's hooves, while al-Hasan and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the jinn feared she would reveal their secrets. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi emphasise his wish to magnify his authority in her eyes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin regard the accounts of the depilatory and the hair removal as Israelite narrations, while al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi transmit them without deciding. Scholars also differ on the marriage: some say Solomon married her or settled her in Syria, others that he gave her in marriage to Dhu Tubba', king of Hamadhan, and al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note no sound proof either way.

This verse tells that God sent to the people of Thamud their brother Salih, who commanded them to worship God alone. When he called them, his people split into two groups, one that believed in him and one that rejected him, each claiming to hold the truth. Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi understand the two groups as believers and disbelievers, while Qatada, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that the two groups may be Salih and his people before any of them believed. According to al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi the dispute concerned whether Salih was truly sent by his Lord, and al-Razi takes it as proof that debate in religious matters is legitimate.

The commentators agree that Salih addressed his people gently and reproached them for seeking punishment before mercy, urging them to ask forgiveness. Mujahid and al-Baghawi take the evil to mean punishment and the good to mean mercy, while as-Suddi takes it as affliction and well-being. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that these people thought they could repent if the punishment came. When they blamed their misfortune on Salih and his companions, he replied that their fate lay with God, according to Ibn Abbas that misfortune comes from God, and according to Qatada that it refers to their deeds recorded with Him. Most explain being tested as being tried by good and evil, while Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir offer other meanings.

According to many commentaries, nine leading men of corruption plotted together to kill Salih and his household. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan describe their oath and how God destroyed them. Al-Razi understands God's scheme as destroying them when they did not expect it. Al-Baydawi sees the empty dwellings as a sign of the ruin of the wrongdoers.

In this verse, the prophet Salih, peace be upon him, asks his people of Thamud, who had split into believers and disbelievers and were quarrelling over him: why do you seek the evil, meaning punishment, before the good, meaning mercy? Why do you not seek forgiveness from God and repent of your disbelief, so that you may be shown mercy? The commentators agree that the evil means punishment and trial, the good means mercy and well-being, and seeking forgiveness here means repenting from polytheism. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others say they were demanding the punishment Salih had threatened, mockingly and defiantly. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the people thought repentance would be accepted once the punishment came, so Salih answered on their own assumptions to expose their error. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read it as an exhortation to seek mercy through faith. Abu Hayyan understands that the punishment was already coming before any repentance. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that repentance is no longer accepted once punishment arrives, hence the need to seek forgiveness beforehand. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i link the good to faith or repentance. Ibn Ashur sees the question as a rebuke and an implicit warning to the Quraysh. All agree that repentance before punishment is the path to mercy.

This passage tells the story of Salih and his people, Thamud. After calling them to worship God alone, they split into two groups, believers and disbelievers. When he urged them to seek forgiveness rather than hasten punishment, they replied that they considered him and those with him a bad omen, since drought had struck them after his coming. Salih answered that whatever good or evil reaches them comes from God, by His decree and measure, not from a bird they observe nor from the prophet and his followers, and that they are in fact a people being tested. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the 'bird' stands for the fate decreed for a person, good or bad, and that 'fitna' means trial. Ibn Abbas and Qatada, cited by several, explain the trial as being tested through good and evil, or through obedience and disobedience. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur also suggest that 'the bird' may mean a person's deeds recorded with God, and that 'fitna' may mean turning away from their religion or being punished for their sins. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi explain that tatayyur comes from the Arab custom of reading omens from the flight of birds, which Islam forbids, with reliance on God as its remedy. The passage then describes nine men who plotted by night to kill Salih and his household, and God's answer was their destruction. The commentaries thus converge on the view that ill omen comes not from the prophets but from God, and that the verse teaches the law of trial and warns against tatayyur.

This verse states that in the city of Thamud, that is al-Hijr where the people of Salih lived, there were nine men of the notables, sons of their leaders, whose activity was spreading corruption on the earth with nothing good mixed into it. The commentators agree that these were the men who conspired to slaughter the she-camel, led by Qudar ibn Salif, who struck her himself. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Kalbi understand the nine as individuals rather than tribes, though the reports giving their names differ widely and are not reliable. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the word rahṭ denotes a group from three to ten. As to the nature of the corruption, opinions differ: Ibn al-Musayyab and Ata said it was clipping and breaking gold and silver coins; Qatada said it was prying into people's faults; others understood it as disbelief and disobedience in general. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di favour a broad reading in which corruption covers every path to evil. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the phrase and they do not set things right means their corruption is unmixed, with no good in it at all. Readers differ on the vocalisation of some words such as tiqasamu and linubayyitannahu: some take them as an imperative reported in speech, others as a past verb in the sense of a circumstance; all agree on the meaning, namely swearing a binding oath to attack Salih and his household by night and then to deny it before his avenger. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that the oath was a way of avoiding an outright lie through equivocation. The accounts of their destruction vary: Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi mention the cry, Ibn Abbas and al-Zamakhshari stones thrown by angels, and Ibn Zayd a rock sealing a cave.

The verse describes nine men of Thamud, leading figures of the people, who spread corruption in the land without ever setting anything right. They swore by God to ambush Salih and his household at night and kill them, then to tell his guardian of blood that they had not witnessed their destruction and were truthful. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that these nine were the ones who hamstrung the she-camel, and that the word tabyit means a surprise attack by night, with "his household" meaning his followers or close family. On the verb taqasamu, most read it as a command to swear, while al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi allow it to be a past verb in a circumstantial sense. The truthfulness of their final statement is more contested: al-Zamakhshari argues that they considered themselves truthful because they had planned both attacks together, whereas Abu Hayyan and al-Shinqiti hold that they were plainly lying, and many exegetes see an equivocation or a customary sense of presence. The readings differ on mahlik, and several scholars explain its possible senses as the act, the time or the place of the destruction. The names of the nine vary widely among the authors, and several consider these details unsupported. As for how they perished, the accounts diverge: angels pelting them with stones (Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid), a rock or a mountain falling on them (Qatada, Muqatil, al-Suddi), or the cry mentioned by Ibn Kathir; Ibn 'Uthaymin reminds that one should stick to what the Quran states.

This verse recounts how the nine men of Thamud plotted secretly to kill the prophet Salih and his family at night, then planned to deny the crime before the avenger of blood. God answered with a greater scheme, striking them unexpectedly when they least expected it. The commentators agree that the human plot was a hidden design, while God's plot was a punishment inflicted by surprise. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd, reports that the men hid in a cave where a rock sealed the entrance; Ibn Abbas and Qatada speak of stones hurled by angels or a rock that crushed them; Muqatil says a mountain collapsed upon them; al-Suddi mentions a landslide into a hollow.
