All agree that the general destruction of the people came through a single cry, and that Salih and the believers were saved. Al-Tabari holds that the readings of the word for "that we" with a short or long vowel are both valid and close in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari explains the oath of the conspirators as a legal stratagem, a view that Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan answer with criticism. Ibn Kathir lists the names of the leaders, including Qudar ibn Salif, who hamstrung the she-camel. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that the empty houses are proof of the punishment deserved by their wrongdoing, and that the verse teaches believers that the end of wrongdoers is ruin.

In this verse God directs the Prophet to reflect on the outcome of the scheme of nine men of Thamud against their prophet Salih. They swore together to attack him and his family by night and then deny any knowledge of it to his heir, and the result was that God destroyed them and all their people. The commentators agree that their plot was this secret conspiracy to kill Salih. On how God foiled them, they differ. Al-Kalbi says angels struck them with stones while they could not see who was throwing them. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd report that they hid in a cave, a rock sealed its mouth, or the mountain collapsed on them, while Qatada speaks of a rock sent down to crush them. Nearly all agree that the general destruction of the people came by a great cry. On the reading of the hamza in 'inna', the Kufan readers use the fatha, making the clause a substitute for the consequence or a cause with the particle removed, while the others read the kasra, starting a new sentence. Al-Tabari judges both readings correct and close in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that 'taqasamu' may be a command to swear or a circumstantial verb. The commentators also describe the wrongdoing of this group, which included disbelief, sins, clipping of coins and prying into women's private affairs, without a single point being singled out as the consensus.

The commentators explain that the verse means that the dwellings of Thamud now stand empty and in ruin, because God destroyed them for their wrongdoing, namely their polytheism and their rejection of their prophet Salih. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the ruin of houses is a punishment that falls on wrongdoers in all the revealed laws. For these scholars, the verse is a lesson for the contemporaries of the Prophet Muhammad who reject him. The word 'khawiyah' is a circumstantial state (hal) or, in the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar, a nominative predicate.

The commentators agree that faith and piety were the cause of the salvation of Salih and those who believed with him, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir state. They differ, however, on how the nine men who plotted to kill Salih perished: according to Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, angels pelted them with stones; according to Qatada, a rock was hurled upon them; according to Muqatil and al-Suddi, a mountain or rock collapsed on them in a cave or at the foot of a hill. Al-Tabari reports that Salih left with the believers for Syria, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi mention Hadramawt.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the wrongdoing as shirk. Al-Razi points out that the lesson benefits only those who have knowledge. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi observe that the accusative reading is the most common.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the account of Thamud's destruction and states that God saved those who believed in Salih and who were mindful of God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi say there were about four thousand of them, and al-Tabari reports that Salih and the believers went to Ramla in Palestine, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy report that Salih died on reaching Hadramawt, which gave the region its name. Ibn 'Ashur regards these accounts of the place as not firmly established. The scholars agree that the cause of salvation is faith combined with piety, meaning guarding against disbelief and sins and obeying God and His messenger. Al-Shaarawi and Ibn Uthaymin take the link between the salvation and these qualities to show that faith and piety are causes of deliverance, and al-Razi adds that the mention of rescue reassures believers that God protects them as He protected earlier believers. On the main meaning there is no disagreement; the differences concern only details of the departure and the destination, which do not change the promise made to the pious believers.

This verse recalls the Prophet Lot rebuking his people for committing the indecency, that is, sodomy, while they knew well its ugliness. The commentators read the phrase "while you see" in two main ways. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it first as sight of the heart, meaning that they knew it was an indecency no one had committed before them. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it as physical sight, since they practised it openly without hiding from one another. Several, including Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, allow both meanings together, and some add the sight of the punishments that struck earlier sinners.

The commentators agree that Lot reproached them for turning away from women, whom God created for lawful desire, in favour of an unnatural appetite. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin link this reproach to parallel passages. On "you are a people who are ignorant", al-Tabari understands foolishness and ignorance of God's right, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi understand ignorance of the Resurrection and of the outcome of disobedience, Abu Hayyan understands ignorance of the end of their conduct, and al-Zamakhshari points to the frivolity and debauchery they indulged in. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Zamakhshari also note the choice of direct address, which they consider the stronger form.

On the sequel, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi report that the people answered by demanding that Lot's family be expelled because they regard themselves as pure, which Mujahid and Qatada take as mockery. On punishment, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi draw from this account an argument for stoning for sodomy, while Malik and others prescribe it regardless of marital status, citing the hadith ordering that the doer and the receiver be killed. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the companions agreed on execution, while the method is left to the ruler's judgement as a deterrent.

This verse records Lot's rebuke to his people for committing a grave indecency: going to men with desire instead of women. The rebuke is sharpened by the rhetorical question and the emphatic particles. The commentators agree that the act is deeply reprehensible and that this people committed it openly without concealment, which made their sin greater. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that they acted out of folly and ignorance of the magnitude of God's right, thereby disobeying His command. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take 'ignorance' to mean acting like people who do not grasp the ugliness of the deed or its consequences, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud understand it as frivolity and debauchery. As for 'while you see', al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan take it as sight of the heart, meaning knowledge of the act's ugliness, or as the fact that they committed it in front of one another; al-Zamakhshari also reads it as observing the traces of earlier sinners. Al-Qurtubi relays the view that the verse supports forbidding the depiction of living beings. Ibn Kathir reports an opinion that makes this offence a ground for execution of both the active and passive partners, and he notes that Lot's wife incited her people against the guests. The overall meaning is clear: a condemnation of an abominable act, whose root is ignorance of God's right.

This verse says that the people of Lot did not answer him with an argument or with acceptance. Instead they agreed among themselves to expel Lot and his household from the town, saying that they are people who purify themselves. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, take this to mean that Lot's people were pure in refraining from anal intercourse with men. Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Qatada, as al-Tabari reports, say this was spoken mockingly, and Qatada adds that they blamed them without any fault. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi offer a different reading in which the phrase means that they keep away from filth and regard the people's act as foul. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that, unable to refute him, the people turned to force and threats. Al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari report that the word qaddarnaha, read in two ways, means that Lot's wife was decreed to be among those who remained behind in punishment. Commentators agree that God rescued Lot and his family except his wife, and that stones rained on the wrongdoers. Ibn Atiyya draws from this verse an argument for those jurists who hold that men who commit sodomy should be stoned, while noting that Malik and others held this view regardless of marital status, and the commentary does not settle the matter.

The commentators explain that this verse reports that God saved Lot and his family except his wife, whom He decreed to be among those who would remain in punishment, meaning those who would perish with their people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that she approved of her people's deeds and aided them, while al-Tabari explains that the phrase means God's decree was made concerning her. Al-Zamakhshari and others note that the readings with and without the doubled letter in the verb carry the same meaning: to judge and decree. All agree that the rain sent upon the people was stones of baked clay, and that the verse ends by stressing the evil of the rain for those who had been warned and refused. The next verse divides the scholars over who is addressed. Al-Farra' and those who follow him hold that Lot is told to praise God for the destruction of his people, whereas al-Nahhas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that it addresses the Prophet Muhammad, who is to praise God for the ruin of the earlier nations. As for "His chosen servants", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them to be the Companions of the Prophet, while Muqatil takes them to be the prophets and messengers, and Ibn Kathir notes that these views do not conflict, since the prophets are included a fortiori. The readings of "yushrikun" vary between the second and third person, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the Prophet would recite, "Rather, God is better, more enduring, more exalted and more generous."

The commentators explain that God saved Lot and his household except his wife, who was destined to be among those who perished, and rained upon his people a rain of stones of baked clay, a dreadful rain for those who had been warned and would not heed. Most of them, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, agree that 'rain' here means the stones that destroyed them after their city was overturned, and that the phrasing stresses the severity and strangeness of the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi recall that this people was punished for the sin of relations between men, and some jurists have seen in the verse a basis for stoning as the penalty for this act, while Malik and others did not extend this to adultery. On the words 'Say: praise be to God, and peace upon His chosen servants', opinions differ over the addressee: al-Farra' takes it as addressed to Lot, while most take it as an instruction to the Prophet to praise God for the destruction of the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Thawri hold that the chosen servants are the Prophet's companions, al-Kalbi that they are the community of Muhammad, and Muqatil that they are the prophets and messengers; these views are not necessarily mutually exclusive. As for 'Is God better, or what they associate with Him?', all read it as a rebuke of the polytheists, the comparison being made in a mocking manner, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to praise Him for the destruction of the deniers and the salvation of the believers, and to greet the servants He has chosen. The commentators differ on who these chosen servants are. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by Abu Malik, al-Suddi and Sufyan al-Thawri, said they are the Companions of the Prophet; al-Kalbi said they are the community of Muhammad; Muqatil and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said they are the prophets and messengers. Ibn Kathir notes there is no contradiction, since the prophets are even more fitting for the description. Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su'ud mention further opinions that include all believers. The verse then asks, 'Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?' Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as a rebuke and a mockery, since nothing good is found in what they associate with Allah, and the comparison serves to make them see their error. Al-Sam'ani notes that Arabs sometimes use this form even when no good is possible on one side, as in a line of Hassan ibn Thabit. Others hold that the comparison follows the belief of the polytheists, who thought their idols brought some benefit. The readings differ between the second and third person plural, and the Prophet is reported to have said upon reciting it: 'Rather, Allah is better, more lasting, more majestic and more noble.' The surah goes on to list God's favours: the creation of the heavens and earth, the sending down of water, the growing of gardens, the mountains and seas, repeating the question 'is there another god with Allah?' to affirm monotheism.

God puts a rhetorical question to the idolaters: is the One who created the heavens and the earth, sent down water from the sky, and caused lush, walled gardens of beauty to grow by it, to be given a partner? The commentators agree that the verse is a proof of God's oneness in creation and in His favours, and that the question is meant to be answered with an admission of the truth. They differ on some words. Al-Hasan understood the gardens to be palm groves, al-Kalbi a walled orchard containing trees and palms, while Qatada and al-Dahhak explained the beauty (bahja) as freshness and splendour. Ibn Abbas and others read "is there a god with God?" as a denial that there is any god beside Him, whereas Zayd ibn Aslam took it as asking whether any partner could do such things. On "ya'dilun", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others understood it as turning away from the truth, whereas Qutrub and Muqatil understood it as making equals to God. Al-Razi observed the shift to the first person plural in "fa-anbatna": God attributes the growth to Himself so that people will not imagine that their own sowing and watering produce it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir conclude that God alone creates and provides, that the idolaters themselves acknowledge this, and that worship therefore belongs to Him alone.

This passage from Surah An-Naml, as explained by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir among others, is a proof of God's oneness following a list of His signs on earth. God made the earth a stable resting place that does not shake with its inhabitants, He made rivers flow through it, He set firm mountains upon it to hold it steady, and He placed between the two seas, the sweet and the salt, a barrier that keeps them from mixing. The question is then put to the idolaters: is there a god with God who did this? The implied answer is no, and the verse ends by saying that most of them do not know the greatness of God. The commentators agree that the interrogation is a rebuke and a challenge, and that the clauses after the word 'amman' continue the argument or replace the earlier phrase. On the word 'qarar', al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain it as stable and not moving, while al-Razi details the benefits of its firmness, density and stillness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress the rivers that run through the land for people's benefit. As for the two seas, al-Dahhak takes them as sweet and salt water, Mujahid as the sky and the earth, al-Hasan as the seas of Persia and Rome, and al-Suddi as those of Iraq and Syria; Ibn 'Atiyya and most scholars prefer the reading of sweet and salt water. All agree that the denial targets any divinity claimed as a rival to God, and that the closing words condemn the heedlessness of the polytheists in the face of clear signs.

This verse asks who, other than God, answers the distressed person when he calls on Him, removes the harm, and makes you successors on the earth, and then asks in rebuke whether there is any god alongside God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God is the one called upon in hardship and hoped for in calamities, and that the idolaters turned to Him alone in distress before returning to their associating. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi state that the mudtarr is the afflicted and exhausted person whom illness, poverty or a calamity has driven to plead. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi list other readings: one with no strength or recourse, the sinner who repents, the wronged person who prays. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi tie the answer to what is beneficial, and al-Razi holds that the phrase denotes a category rather than every individual, so not every distressed person is answered. Most commentators take the harm to be bodily or material distress, while al-Kalbi takes it as injustice. On succession, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand generations following one another, al-Naqqash understands one's children, and al-Kalbi understands unbelievers settling the land after their destruction. Abu 'Amr reads the verb with the yā', while the rest read it with the tā', and most see the final phrase as a statement of scant reflection. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the argument moves from cosmic signs to human states of need, adversity and benefit from the earth.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the One who guides people through the darkness of land and sea, and who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy, meaning the rain, is God alone, so no other god can be set alongside Him, and God is exalted above what they associate with Him. There is broad agreement that the darknesses are the nights on land and at sea, when travellers are guided by the stars at night and by landmarks by day, as Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi state. Al-Tabari reads these darknesses as losing the way, while Ibn Juzayy adds guidance by the stars and by roads. Al-Mawardi gives two readings of the guidance: directing travellers along their routes, or rescuing them from the terrors of land and sea, the second reported from al-Suddi. He also notes differing views on land and sea, some taking them as earth and water, others as the desert of the Bedouins and the cities, reported from al-Dahhak. On the word bushran, Ibn Abbas reads it as bringing good tidings, al-Suddi as scattering, and Yahya ibn Salam as fertilising. Al-Razi gives a long account of how winds arise from rising vapours, then answers the objections of the philosophers by holding that every cause is created by God. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi take the mercy to be the rain. Ibn Ashur notes that the guidance is by the stars and that the verse closes by declaring God free of association, as a summary of the argument.

In this verse God challenges the polytheists: is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the sky with rain and from the earth with plants, a god alongside Allah? The Prophet is told to demand their proof if they are truthful. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, agree that the repetition means resurrection after death, and that the provision refers to rain from the sky and vegetation from the earth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the argument stands even though the idolaters deny resurrection, because they acknowledge the original creation, which makes the return obvious and leaves them no excuse. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the question is confirmatory in form, and that provision is linked to creation in meaning. Al-Razi notes that the question about resurrection is addressed to those who deny it as if they admitted it. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya read the command to bring proof as a rebuke and a challenge, while al-Alusi sees irony in the phrasing. The verse belongs to a series of arguments for divine oneness and prepares the next verse, which states that none in the heavens and earth knows the unseen except Allah, and that the idolaters do not perceive when they will be raised. These commentaries agree that the verse establishes God's oneness through clear evidence and leaves the associators no valid argument.

God commands His Prophet to say that no one in the heavens or on earth knows the unseen, which belongs to God alone, including the hour of the Resurrection, so those in the heavens and on earth do not know when they will be raised. The verse answers the Quraysh who asked the Prophet about the Hour. The commentators agree that God alone knows the unseen, and some, such as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi quoting 'Aisha, use it to reject any claim to knowledge of the future. The nominative form of the divine name despite the discontinuous exception is explained by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi as a feature of Tamimi usage, while Ibn al-Qayyim argues it is a continuous exception. On the reading "bal idarak", Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean their knowledge has ended, vanished or failed to reach them, whereas al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Zajjaj understand that their knowledge of the Hereafter will be complete on the Day of Resurrection, yet of no benefit to them. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note that the disbelievers are in doubt about the Hereafter and blind to it. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the successive stages a progression from ignorance to blindness.

This passage affirms that knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone: no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Him, and they do not know when they will be raised. The commentators then describe the state of those who deny the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Tabari, Muqatil and others explain (bal adraka 'ilmuhum) as meaning that their knowledge of the Hereafter becomes complete when they witness it, yet this knowledge will not benefit them, since they were deniers in worldly life. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Qutayba take it to mean that their knowledge has vanished and perished. Mujahid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi read (bal) as equivalent to (am) and the sentence as a question: has their knowledge reached the knowledge of the Hereafter? The implied answer is no. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj see mockery in ascribing perfect knowledge to them. The majority read (idda-raka), meaning succession or accumulation, while Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (adraka), meaning to reach. Al-Farra' takes (fi) to mean (ba). Al-Tabari notes that their doubt about the Hereafter persisted in this life and that they were blind to it. Ibn Kathir states that the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, even though the wording refers to all creatures. The commentators agree that the three successive turns of the sentence describe rising degrees: no awareness of the time of resurrection, weakness of knowledge, doubt, and finally blindness.

The verse reports the disbelievers' denial of resurrection: they ask, astonished, whether they will be brought out alive from their graves once they and their fathers have become dust. Al-Tabari explains that they mean being brought out of the graves in their own form after death, and that they consider the promise to have been made before Muhammad ﷺ and to their forefathers without any reality being seen, so they call it the fables of the ancients, meaning falsehoods written down by earlier generations. The commentators agree that the verse expresses the polytheists' astonishment and rejection of resurrection, and that the question carries the force of denial. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain the double emphasis as an intensification of the refusal, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan describe it as denial upon denial. On grammar and recitation, the scholars differ: Nafi' reads 'idha' with a single hamza, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read 'inna' with two nuns as a statement, while Asim, Hamza and Abu 'Amr keep the repeated interrogation. Grammarians note that 'idha' cannot be governed by 'mukhrajun' because of the hamza, 'inna' and the lam, so they supply an implied verb, 'nakhruju'. Al-Razi observes that placing 'hadha' first shows that resurrection itself is the main object of the denial, and al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur link the word order to the purpose of the speech. The sources agree that the following verses answer them by commanding a journey through the earth to see the fate of the criminals.

This verse records the words of the Meccan disbelievers who denied the resurrection: we and our fathers were promised this before, but it is nothing but the fables of the ancients. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the disbelievers found it impossible that bodies turned to dust could be brought back to life, and they rejected the message by claiming they had never seen any reality behind the promise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'the fables of the ancients' refers to tales written down and passed on without any basis. Al-Qurtubi notes that the prophets stressed how near the Day was, since whatever is coming is close. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi point out that placing 'this' before 'we and our fathers' shows that the resurrection itself is the main subject, whereas in Surat al-Mu'minun the reverse order puts the focus on the people raised. Readers differ on the recitation of 'idha' and 'a-inna': Abu Ubayd prefers the reading of Nafi, while Abu Hayyan explains why 'mukhrajun' cannot govern 'idha' because of the interrogative particle and the particle inna. Ibn 'Ashur sees a tone of mockery in the disbelievers' emphatic questions. The following verses call people to travel the earth and look at the fate of the criminals, and console the Prophet over their scheming.

God commands His Prophet to tell the disbelievers to travel through the earth and see what became of the criminals, meaning those who denied the messengers. Al-Tabari explains that God destroyed their peoples, left their dwellings empty, and that this is His way with anyone who follows their path. The commentators understand the word "criminals" as referring to the disbelievers, and many note that using this label also warns believers away from sin. God then consoles the Prophet, forbidding him to grieve over their turning away or to feel constricted by their schemes, since God will support him against them. When the pagans ask when this promise will come, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Abbas take the verb to mean "it has drawn near to you", while al-Farra' treats the lam as an added particle. Most identify the punishment as the battle of Badr, while others point to the punishment of the grave. Al-Razi notes that the question is mocking and that God delays the punishment out of grace. The exegetes also record differing readings and opinions on the phrase about their knowledge of the Hereafter, some reading it as blame and others as praise.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ, telling him not to grieve over the disbelievers who turn away from him and deny him, and not to feel constricted by their schemes. The commentators agree that the message is one of consolation and reassurance: God is his helper and will make his religion prevail over them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri explain that the grief concerns their persistence in disbelief, that the constriction is the tightness of the heart in the face of their plotting, and that God protects His Prophet from people. Al-Jaza'iri adds that the plot aimed at killing him and did not succeed. Ibn 'Ashur links the command to the Prophet's deep compassion for his community, which made reassurance necessary. Ibn Sa'di adds that had he known the evil within them, he would not have grieved. The exegetes see the verse as part of the warning that precedes it, where he is told to travel the earth and see the fate of the wrongdoers. On recitation, Ibn Kathir reads «ḍīq» with a kasra, while the others read it with a fatha; both are verbal nouns with the same meaning. Al-Zamakhshari allows that the word may also mean a distressing matter. The overall sense remains: do not grieve, and let your heart not be constricted, for God will support you and bring them to ruin.

The verse reports that the disbelievers asked, mockingly and impatiently, when the threatened punishment would come, if the Prophet and his followers were truthful. The reply comes in the form of a hope: "Perhaps some of what you are seeking to hasten has drawn near to you." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain the verb "radifa" as "drew near" or "hastened". Ibn Qutayba, cited by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes it to mean "followed", regarding the lam as superfluous, a view al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi also report. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi say the lam is added for emphasis, or that the verb carries the sense of "approached", which requires that preposition.

Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Sudi and Ibn Kathir, identify this part as the punishment of the Battle of Badr. Al-Mawardi also mentions the punishment of the grave. The exegetes agree that the words "asa", "la'alla" and "sawfa" used by kings in their promises and threats express certainty and dignity rather than doubt; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Razi see in them a way of making a promise firm. Several note God's mercy in saying "some" rather than "all", and al-Qasimi and Ibn Kathir stress that God's favour reaches even the disbelievers, though most do not give thanks. Ibn Ashur notes that the present tense shows this speech was repeated.

God instructs His Prophet to answer the disbelievers who ask when the threatened punishment will come: perhaps, he says, part of what you are hastening for has already drawn near to you. The commentators explain that the verb radifa means to draw near or be close, as Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' report, while others read it as to follow closely or to hasten for you, as Mujahid says. Most identify the part that is near as the punishment they suffered at Badr through death and capture, whereas al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the punishment of the grave.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that 'asa, la'alla and sawfa, when used in the promises and threats of kings, express the certainty and seriousness of the matter, and that the choice of such words is meant to display dignity and confidence in their power; God's promise and threat follow the same pattern. Grammarians differ over the preposition li after the verb: some consider it superfluous for emphasis, while others take it as implying the sense of drawing near.

Commentators connect the verse to what follows. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that God shows grace to people by delaying the punishment, though most of them do not give thanks; that He knows what their hearts conceal and what they display; and that nothing hidden in heaven or earth escapes the Clear Book.

The commentators explain that God is full of favour towards people: He delays their punishment for their sins and disbelief rather than seizing them at once. Yet most of them do not recognise the worth of this blessing or thank Him for it through faith and sincere worship, and out of ignorance they even ask for the punishment to hasten. Ibn 'Abbas and others report that the address concerns the pagans of Quraysh who asked when this promise would come; God answers that some of what they seek to hasten is near. Most exegetes identify this as the Battle of Badr, while others take it to be the punishment of the grave.

The commentators agree that God knows what hearts conceal and what is made public, and that His knowledge encompasses everything hidden in the heavens and the earth, all recorded in a clear Book, which most identify as the Preserved Tablet. Al-Mawardi also gives the alternative of the decree that cannot be reversed. Al-Hasan takes the hidden thing to mean the Day of Resurrection, whereas Ibn Shajara takes it to mean everything God has concealed from His creatures.

The commentators differ on the sense of the speech attributed to the beast mentioned in the following verses. Some understand that it will speak to people, others that it will wound them or mark their faces. They do not decide between these readings and present each where it belongs.

The commentators explain that God knows what the hearts conceal and what people openly display, and nothing is hidden from Him. Al-Tabari understands it as the inner thoughts, hidden secrets and visible deeds, all of which God records in order to repay each person. Ibn Jurayj takes what is concealed to mean secret matters. Ibn Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the verb to mean concealing and hiding, and they apply it to the hostility of the disbelievers towards the Prophet ﷺ and their plots, which God knows and for which He will requite them. A minority reading, recorded from Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd, vocalises it with a fatha on the first letter, giving the same sense.

Most exegetes place the verse in the context of consoling the Prophet ﷺ and warning those who deny him. If God delays their punishment, it is not because He is unaware of their condition, but because there is an appointed term, as al-Nasafi puts it, and this delay is a favour, as al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note. Al-Razi observes that the mention of what is in the hearts precedes what is expressed, since inner intentions are the cause of visible acts.

Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi note that the verse implies the disbelievers harbour other designs beyond those reported, such as plans against the Prophet and the believers. Ibn Sa'di draws from it a general warning that each person should guard against keeping in the heart what displeases God, since His knowledge embraces the hidden as well as the apparent.

This verse states that God's knowledge encompasses everything hidden and unseen in the heavens and the earth, and that all of it is recorded in a clear Book. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify this clear Book as the Preserved Tablet, in which God has written everything that will happen from the creation until the Day of Resurrection. They explain that the 'unseen' refers to anything concealed from human eyes. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says that nothing, whether secret or public, in the heavens and the earth is unknown to God. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record other meanings: for al-Hasan the unseen is the Day of Judgment, for others the hidden punishment of heaven and earth, and for Ibn Shajara everything God has kept from His creatures. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that the feminine ending intensifies the meaning, so the phrase means something deeply hidden, and that the Book may be the Tablet or the irrevocable decree. Ibn 'Ashur reads the Book as a figure for God's unchanging knowledge, and 'clear' as meaning detailed and evident.

The commentators agree that the verse serves as a concluding statement stressing the breadth of God's knowledge, and that the punishment the disbelievers demand is known and fixed with God even though it remains hidden from creation. Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the verse to the context of the surah, seeing in it both a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya also reports that Aisha cited this verse to deny that the dead of Badr heard the Prophet, while he himself holds that the verse does not contradict the specific cases in which the dead are said to hear.

This verse states that the Quran relates to the Children of Israel most of what they disputed, setting it out correctly and removing the grounds of their disagreement. Most commentators see the chief example as the dispute over Jesus, where some exalted him to divinity and others slandered him, and the Quran gives the true account. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the disputes also covered other matters, such as God's attributes and the Resurrection. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi extend it to legal rulings and to the distortions in the Torah and the Gospel. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur see the Quran's agreement with earlier scriptures as evidence of its divine origin, Ibn 'Ashur citing the story of the Queen of Sheba as an example. All agree that the Quran is guidance and mercy for believers, who alone benefit from it. Regarding God's judgment between the parties, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi place it on the Day of Resurrection, while al-Qurtubi notes it may also take place in this world through exposing what was altered. The verse closes by consoling the Prophet: since he stands on clear truth, he should trust in God. The commentators explain that those who refuse to listen are like the dead, the deaf and the blind, so his call cannot reach them.

This verse describes the Quran as guidance and mercy, and the commentators explain that it is specified for believers because they are the ones who benefit from it. It follows the Quranic statement that the Children of Israel differed on many matters, including Jesus, and that the Quran clarifies the truth about them. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi say that God will judge between the disputants on the Day of Judgment by His just rule, while al-Qurtubi reports that this judgment may also take place in this world by exposing what had been distorted. Al-Razi notes that the attributes of might and knowledge accompany the judgment to guarantee its execution and its correctness.

The commentators agree that the following verses comfort the Prophet, who is told to put his trust in God because he stands upon the manifest truth. Those who reject him are compared to the dead, the deaf and the blind, who gain nothing from what they hear or see. Al-Tabari reads this as hearts sealed by God, while Ibn Kathir reads it as a punishment for hardened hearts. Al-Razi explains that the comparison cuts off the Prophet's hope that they will believe, which strengthens his resolve in preaching.

Opinions differ on who the dead are. Some identify them as the disbelievers, others take the image more broadly, and al-Shinqiti recalls the scholarly debate on whether the dead can hear. The majority sense is that only those who believe in these signs benefit from the message, and that they are the ones who submit to God.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment your Lord will decide between those who disagree, first among them the Children of Israel, by His just judgment. He is the Mighty, whose ruling cannot be overturned, and the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that God will repay the righteous and the wrongdoer according to what each deserves, punishing the transgressor and rewarding the one who does good. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take "by His judgment" to mean by His justice, since He judges only with equity, or by His wisdom, a reading supported by the variant "bi-hikamih". Al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that the Qur'an sets out the truth about what the Children of Israel disputed, and that God then separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong.

The commentators agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ: the Qur'an has clarified what divided the Children of Israel, and the final judgment belongs to God alone. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur also read in it an encouragement to believers who grow impatient for victory, since the divine judgment will distinguish the two camps. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that this judgment combines knowledge and power: knowledge guarantees correctness, power guarantees execution. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri add that this judgment may concern the Hereafter or this world, through the disclosure of what had been altered, as al-Qurtubi also reports.

The verse belongs to a larger passage: it is followed by a command to put one's trust in God, and by a description of those who turn away from the truth as dead, deaf and blind, of whom only those who believe in God's signs truly hear.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to put his trust in God and not to concern himself with the hostility of his people, because he stands upon the clear truth. The commentators explain that this call to tawakkul rests on two reasons. First, one who holds the truth deserves to rely on God's protection and support, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir state. Second, the disbelievers do not benefit from the message and are likened to the dead, the deaf and the blind, so the Prophet must give up hoping for their support. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the comparison with the dead means they gain nothing from what is recited to them, that a deaf person who turns away hears even less, and that the guidance denied to the Prophet is the guidance of success rather than of pointing the way.

The exegetes agree that the verse consoles the Prophet and that the turning away of opponents does not diminish the truth. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di hold that these people's hearts are closed to guidance, while al-Shawkani notes that the verse denies only useful hearing, not hearing in general. On whether the dead can hear, some cite this verse to deny it, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya rely on the hadith of the well of Badr and al-Qurtubi cites reports that the dead hear. Ibn 'Atiyya regards the Badr episode as an exceptional breach of custom granted to the Prophet, and Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the hearing denied is the hearing that leads to acceptance and response.

The recitation and grammar of the verse also vary, such as Hamza's reading « wa ma anta tahdi al-'umya » against the majority's « bi-hadi al-'umy », reported by Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi. The commentaries also discuss the creature that will emerge when the word takes effect against the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi record the differences about its form and place of emergence, while al-Qurtubi favours one view, though these details are not settled in this passage.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ: he cannot make the truth heard by those whose hearts are dead to faith, who are like the dead, nor make the deaf hear his call when they turn away and leave, nor guide the blind out of their error. Only those who believe in God's signs hear and reflect, and submit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a consolation for the Prophet and a reason to trust God: these people's misguidance does not diminish the truth he brings. Opinions differ on the meaning of "the dead": Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take them to be the disbelievers, while al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya see a comparison with those who gain nothing from what they hear, and al-Shawkani describes people sound in their senses who do not benefit from them. On whether the dead hear in their graves, Aisha cites this verse to deny it, whereas Ibn Umar reports the hadith of the Badr well; al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Taymiyya conclude that the authentic hadith establishes some hearing, and that the verse refers to useful hearing. Ibn Atiyya and others add that the guidance denied is guidance of success rather than of pointing the way. About the beast due to emerge at the end of time, the reports differ on its form and place of emergence, Safa in Mecca, Tihama or elsewhere, and several commentators leave the matter open. On readings, Ibn Kathir reads "does not make the deaf hear" and Hamza reads "you guide the blind".

The commentators explain that the Prophet ﷺ cannot guide those whom God has left blind to the truth and whose insight He has closed, and that he can only make himself heard in a way that benefits those who believe in God's signs and submit to them; these are the 'submitters', the believers who yield. The readers differ on 'bihadi al-‘umy': the majority read it as an annexed noun, while Hamza reads the verb 'tahdi al-‘umya'. Al-Tabari judges the two readings close in meaning and both correct. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi see the verse as consolation to the Prophet about his people, following the comparison with the dead, the deaf and the blind, and take the denied hearing to be the hearing that benefits. Ibn Kathir holds that the disbelievers have a veil over their hearts and deafness in their ears, and that those who profit from the call are those who have hearing and sight of the heart. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand 'tusmi'' as hearing with understanding and acceptance, and 'fa-hum muslimun' as a reason for their faith, meaning they submit to the truth, or that they are sincere toward God. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report differences of reading over 'tukallimuhum' and 'anna al-nas', and about the beast to come out: some take its speech literally, others take it as marking believer and disbeliever. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin read 'the dead' as the dead of heart, and the one who turns away from truth as deprived of beneficial hearing; whether the dead hear in their graves is debated by scholars and is not settled by this verse.

The commentators explain that 'when the word falls upon them' means the approach of the threatened punishment. They differ on what 'the word' is: Qatada and al-Tabari take it as anger or punishment; Mujahid as the decree that they will not believe; Ibn Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri as the abandonment of commanding right and forbidding wrong; Abu al-'Aliya as what was revealed to Noah, that none of his people would believe. Most exegetes count the beast among the signs of the Hour that will emerge from the earth, but they differ widely on its appearance and place of emergence. Ibn Abbas describes it as feathered and downy with four legs; Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Jurayj describe a composite of many animals; Ibn Umar places its emergence at Safa in Mecca. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that many reports on the subject exist but most have weak chains. Ibn Kathir reports Ali denying that it had a tail, and al-Qurtubi rejects the view that it is a man debating the heretics. On 'speaking to them', Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada say it will address them; al-Sudi says it will proclaim the falsehood of all religions except Islam; Ibn Abbas in another report says it will wound them, and he concludes that it does both, speaking to the believer and marking the unbeliever. The readings differ: Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'anna' with fatha, the majority 'inna' with kasra. In the next verse the commentators describe each community being gathered as a group of deniers, ordered in rank and questioned: 'Did you deny My signs without encompassing them in knowledge?' Then they fall silent. The passage ends with the sign of night and day as proof of resurrection: sleep resembles death and waking resembles resurrection, and only believers benefit because they reflect.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when a troop will be gathered from every community of those who denied Allah's signs, and the first of them will be held back until the last have joined them before they are driven on. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi agree that a 'fawj' is a large company and that 'yuzaʿun' means being held back or pushed, expressing the vastness of their number and the spread of the crowd. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take the first 'min' as partitive, since every community contains believers and disbelievers, and the second as explanatory. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi also understand the group to be the leaders and chiefs of disbelief, driven ahead of their followers, and al-Zamakhshari names Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a as examples. As for the 'signs', al-Suddi takes them to mean the Prophet, most scholars take them to be all the messengers, and al-Razi holds that they cover all signs.

The commentators then report the rebuke addressed to them on arrival: 'Did you deny My signs without encompassing them in knowledge?' On the meaning of this phrase opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as meaning that they did not truly know them, while Ibn al-Jawzi also offers the sense that they did not reflect on their truth, and Abu Hayyan notes that the 'wa' may be circumstantial or coordinating. Ibn Atiyya and al-Shawkani record a different reading of the interrogative particle. The scene ends with the sentence taking effect because of their wrongdoing, so that they cannot speak, according to most exegetes. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Ashur see in this gathering a special assembly of those who denied, distinct from the general gathering of all creation.

This passage of Surah An-Naml describes the Day of Resurrection, when a group is gathered from every community among those who denied God's signs, and the first of them are held back until the last have caught up before they are driven to judgment. The commentators explain that God rebukes them on arrival: 'Did you deny My signs without grasping them in knowledge? Then what were you doing?' This is a question of reproach rather than a request for information. The exegetes agree that the 'signs' are the revelation and the Quran. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that they denied without knowledge or reflection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan hold that the waw marks a circumstance, and that the question may be meant to silence them, since their only activity was denial. On the verb 'yuza'un', Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean being pushed back, Qatada to mean that the first are held until the last catch up, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi to mean being driven forward, and al-Farra' to mean being gathered into ranks. Those who do not speak are those upon whom the word has come into effect because of their wrongdoing, that is, their polytheism and denial, so they have no argument. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya add that they fall silent during some phases of the Resurrection and speak in others. Finally, the commentators note that the alternation of night and day is a sign of God's power and of resurrection for a people who believe.

The plain meaning of the verse is that the word of punishment falls upon the deniers because of their wrongdoing, namely their denial of God's signs, and that they are then unable to speak or offer any excuse because no proof remains for them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this as the gathering and questioning on the Day of Resurrection, with wrongdoing meaning associating partners with God and denying the signs. Qatada asks how they could speak when they have no argument. Others, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, say their mouths will be sealed. Al-Baydawi explains that the torment that overtakes them keeps them from answering. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the question about their denial as a rebuke, reproaching them for rejecting what they had not grasped. The commentators differ on how far the silence extends: Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di tie it to one particular moment, while Ibn 'Ashur, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the Qur'an elsewhere describes them speaking at other stages of the Last Day, so the silence applies to some stages only. The scholars do not settle between these readings; they set out the views and leave the reader to weigh the evidence.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds those who deny God's signs of a sign they see every day: God made the night a time of stillness, in which people rest from the toil of the day, and made the day bright so that they can see and go about their livelihoods. The alternation of night and day is therefore a proof of the Creator's power and of the possibility of resurrection, although only those who believe are truly moved by it. Most exegetes keep to this plain sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Sa'di see the night as rest and the day as light for seeing, and draw from this proof of God's oneness and of resurrection after death. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the word "mubsiran" (giving sight) is matched in meaning with "li-yaskunu": the sense is that they may see in it the paths of seeking gain. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur follow this reading, seeing an ellipsis and a balance between the two clauses. Al-Razi notes that seeing is attributed to the day by metonymy, since the day is the time of seeing, and that the primary purpose is rest, with sight serving as a means to benefit. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that the mention of believers indicates that they alone benefit from these signs, though the signs are valid for everyone. Al-Alusi takes the seeing as intellectual and sees in the verse a proof of God's unity and of resurrection. The differences concern rhetoric and grammar rather than the basic meaning.

This passage describes the trumpet blast on the Day of Resurrection, when all in the heavens and the earth are seized with terror to the point of fainting, except those God excepts, and every creature comes to Him in humiliation. The commentators agree that the Sur is a horn into which Israfil blows, and that the terror occurs at the blast. Most treat the blowing as literal rather than as a mere image. Ibn Kathir, citing the hadith of Abu Hurayra, speaks of three blasts, while others such as al-Qurtubi and al-Qushayri hold that there are only two. On who is excepted, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say they are the martyrs, who are alive with their Lord, while Muqatil names Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death, and al-Dahhak names the houris, the guardians of Hell and the bearers of the Throne. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that Musa may be among them, since he fainted once. Al-Tabari explains that coming means appearing before the place of judgment or submitting to God's command. Hamza and Hafs read the verb in the past tense, while the majority read the active participle, and al-Tabari considers both readings equivalent. The following verse, in which the mountains pass like clouds, is taken by most to refer to the Day of Resurrection, though some see in it a reference to the motion of the earth. The verse then states that whoever brings a good deed will receive better than it and will be safe from terror, while whoever brings an evil deed will be thrown face down into the Fire. Most commentators identify the good deed with the testimony that there is no god but God, and the evil deed with polytheism.

This verse describes a scene from the terrors of the Day of Resurrection: whoever looks at the mountains thinks them fixed, yet they pass by like clouds. The commentators explain that this appearance comes from their vast size and number, since huge bodies moving in one direction seem almost motionless; some cite the line of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di describing a great army. Most exegetes place this movement on the Last Day, after the trumpet blast, while al-Mawardi reports that it may be a parable, offering three readings: the present world, faith, or the soul at the moment of departure. They agree that "the work of God" is an emphatic expression, and that "who perfected everything" means He made all things firm and well-formed, and that He is aware of what you do. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others transmit the reading of the verb in the following phrase by some Qur'an reciters. Al-Qurtubi and al-Qushayri hold that this movement will happen on the Last Day, whereas al-Sha'rawi sees the mountains' motion as following that of the earth, imperceptible to us. Ibn Ashur reads the verse as an invitation to reflect on the subtle order of creation, without seeing a destruction of the universe. The main disagreement concerns when this movement occurs, not the perfection of God's work.

This passage describes the fate of people on the Day of Resurrection, when the Trumpet is blown: whoever is in the heavens and on earth will be struck with terror, except those whom God exempts, and all will come before Him humbled. The mountains, which seem motionless, will pass like clouds, the work of God who perfected everything. Then comes the recompense: whoever brings a good deed will receive better than it and will be safe from that terror, while whoever brings an evil deed will be thrown face-down into the Fire. Commentators such as Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, Mujahid and Qatada largely agree that the good deed is the profession 'There is no god but God' and the evil deed is polytheism, though Qatada speaks of sincerity and Zayd ibn Aslam of performing all the obligations. On the phrase 'better than it', Ibn Abbas understands that good reaches the doer through the deed; Ibn Jurayj and Ikrima say nothing is better than the declaration of faith; al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and Muhammad ibn Ka'b understand a tenfold multiplication; and al-Razi refers to beholding God's face. The readings differ on 'fear of that day', with or without tanwin; al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd prefer the annexed form as more general, while Abu 'Ali al-Farisi holds that both carry the same meaning. The exceptions from the terror are, according to various views, the martyrs (Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr), the angels (Muqatil), or the houris (al-Dahhak). Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold for two blasts, the terror and the death, then the resurrection, while others count three. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi distinguish the initial dread that no one can avoid from the fear of punishment, which belongs to those who did wrong.

This verse describes the fate of those who come on the Day of Resurrection bearing an evil deed, which most commentators understand as shirk (associating others with God), as al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. It is set against the previous verse, in which whoever brings a good deed, for them the declaration that there is no god but God, receives something better. Those who meet God in polytheism will be thrown into the Fire on their faces, as al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain, and they will be told in rebuke: are you recompensed for anything other than what you used to do?
Most exegetes agree that the evil deed here is shirk, and al-Shawkani and Ibn Ashur base this on the address made to the wrongdoers. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the face is singled out for its honour and that the phrase covers the whole body. Ibn Kathir adds that one who meets God without good deeds, or whose evil deeds outweigh his good, receives the same fate. Al-Razi and al-Alusi report that the Murji'a and the Mu'tazila drew arguments from the verse concerning the sinning believer, and al-Alusi answers that the term means shirk according to the early scholars.
Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a summary conclusion to the warnings before it, while Ibn Uthaymin holds that repaying people with their own deeds is a form of justice, and maintains that the disbeliever is punished both for his unbelief and for his sins.

God commands His Prophet to tell his people that he has been ordered to worship the Lord of this city, that is Mecca, who made it a sanctuary, where no blood may be shed, no one wronged, no game hunted and no tree cut. To Him belongs everything, and the Prophet has been commanded to be among those who submit. The commentators agree that the city is Mecca and that its attribution to God is an honour. Ibn Abbas takes it to mean Mecca, while Abu al-Aliya understands it as Mina, as al-Mawardi reports. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that making it sacred means honouring its sanctity and forbidding hunting and cutting trees there, and that the words 'and to Him belongs everything' prevent the idea that God's lordship is limited to this city.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that this sanctity is a favour to the Quraysh, who lived safely in a land full of unrest. Ibn Atiyya explains that God is said to have made it sacred through His decree and foreknowledge, while the Prophet's saying that Abraham made it sacred refers to Abraham's supplication and proclamation, so there is no contradiction. Ibn Kathir adds that it is sacred both by divine decree and by religious law.

On the rest of the verse, the commentators agree that the Prophet is to recite the Quran, that whoever is guided benefits himself, and that whoever goes astray harms only himself. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi report that this passage was abrogated by the verse of fighting, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Jaza'iri and al-Mahalli consider it not abrogated but addressed to deniers. Finally, the promise that God will show His signs is understood by Mujahid as signs in the sky and in the self, by al-Hasan as signs in the hereafter, and by Ibn Atiyya as punishments in this world such as Badr.

God instructs His Prophet to declare that he has been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who made it a sanctuary and to whom all things belong, to be among those who submit, and to recite the Quran. Whoever is guided benefits only himself, and whoever goes astray is only warned by the Prophet. The commentators agree that the city is Mecca, and that its sanctity means that fighting, hunting its game and cutting its trees are forbidden; calling it the Lord's city is an honour, and the words 'to Him belongs everything' prevent the idea that His lordship is confined to that place. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan link this sanctity to God's decree from the creation of the heavens and the earth. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya attribute it to God because it stems from His decree and knowledge, while the Prophet attributed it to Abraham in a hadith; Ibn Juzayy and others reconcile the two by saying Abraham made it known. On recitation, al-Hasan takes it to mean acting on the Quran, while al-Shawkani and others understand it as recitation accompanied by following. As for the phrase 'I am only a warner', al-Nahhas, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Suyuti consider it abrogated by the verse of fighting, whereas Ibn Kathir and others see it as the fulfilment of the duty to convey the message. The promised 'signs' are read by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid as signs in this world such as the smoke and the splitting of the moon, or sustenance; by al-Hasan as signs of the hereafter; and by al-Baghawi and others as the battle of Badr. Several commentators conclude that the Lord is never unaware of what people do.

God tells His Messenger to say that he has been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, Mecca, who made it sacred, and to whom all things belong, and to be among those who submit to God, and to recite the Quran. Whoever is guided is guided for his own sake, and whoever goes astray, the Prophet's duty is only to warn. He is then told to praise God and to say that God will show them His signs, and they will recognise them. The commentators agree that the city is Mecca and that its sanctity means the protection of its precincts from fighting, hunting and cutting trees, though al-Mawardi reports disagreement over whether the sacred zone includes Mina. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that attributing this sanctity to God does not contradict the Prophet's saying that Abraham made Mecca sacred, since Abraham proclaimed it through his prayer and his preaching. The following verses describe the Day of Gathering, the blast on the Trumpet, and the fate of the mountains, then the reward for the good deed, which most exegetes take to be the declaration that there is no god but God, and the punishment for the evil deed, which is associated partnership with God. As for the signs to be shown, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil refer them to events in this world such as Badr, the smoke and the splitting of the moon, al-Hasan places them in the afterlife, and Mujahid also includes signs within the self and in the horizons. Readers differ on whether the verb at the end is read in the second or third person. Al-Nahhas and Ibn 'Ashur note that some regard the verse of the sword as abrogating the command to only warn, a view that Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur do not accept. All agree that God is never unaware of what people do.
